Think of a **dictionary with thumb tabs**. To find words starting with "ip" you don't read the whole dictionary; you jump to the "I" tab, then the "ip" pages. Now imagine someone has also written, at the top of every page, a **sticky note**: "Most looked-up words on this page: iphone 15, iphone 15 pro, iphone cover". You don't even need to read the page. You just read the sticky note.

That is the whole trick:
- The **tabs** are the **trie**: a way to jump straight to everything that starts with what you typed.
- The **sticky notes** are the **precomputed top-k lists**: the best k suggestions (k is a small number like 5 or 10) already written down at each prefix.
- The person who writes the sticky notes overnight is the **offline build job** that reads search logs.

Terms used below:
- **Prefix**: the beginning part of a word. "iph" is a prefix of "iphone".
- **Query log / search log**: a record of what users searched for, when, and what they clicked or bought afterwards.
- **Latency**: the time between pressing a key and seeing the result.
- **Cache**: a fast store of answers already computed, so you don't compute them again.
- **CDN (Content Delivery Network)**: servers spread across many cities that keep copies of responses close to users. A user in Chennai is served from a nearby server instead of a distant data centre.

## How it actually works

### 1. The trie, drawn small

Say our whole log has only five searches, with how many times each was searched last week:

| Query | Searches |
|---|---|
| iphone 15 | 900 |
| iphone 15 pro | 700 |
| iphone cover | 400 |
| ipad | 300 |
| ipl jersey | 250 |

A trie stores these by sharing common beginnings. Every query starting with "i" hangs under one "i" node, every one starting with "ip" under one "ip" node, and so on. Each node below also shows its stored top list:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R[root] --> I[i]
  I --> IP[ip  top: iphone 15, iphone 15 pro, iphone cover]
  IP --> IPH[iph  top: iphone 15, iphone 15 pro, iphone cover]
  IP --> IPA[ipa  top: ipad]
  IP --> IPL[ipl  top: ipl jersey]
  IPH --> PHONE[iphone  ...]
  PHONE --> P15[iphone 15  top: iphone 15, iphone 15 pro]
  PHONE --> COV[iphone c  top: iphone cover]
```

Looking up "iph" means: start at root, go to "i", then "p", then "h". That is **3 steps, one per letter typed**, no matter whether the trie holds 5 queries or 50 million. That is why a trie fits autocomplete so well.

### 2. Store the top-k at every node

A plain trie still has a problem. To answer "i", you'd have to visit **every** word below "i" (could be millions), then sort them by popularity. Far too slow.

The fix: when building the trie, **store at each node the top k completions** (say k = 10) for that prefix. Now:
- Lookup cost = walk down L letters + read a list of 10. Effectively constant.
- Cost moved to **build time** and **memory**: each node holds a small list.

```java
class TrieNode {
    Map<Character, TrieNode> children = new HashMap<>();
    List<String> topK = new ArrayList<>(); // precomputed, best first
}

List<String> suggest(TrieNode root, String prefix) {
    TrieNode node = root;
    for (char c : prefix.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
        node = node.children.get(c);
        if (node == null) return List.of(); // nobody ever searched this
    }
    return node.topK; // already ranked, nothing to sort
}
```

How the top-k lists are filled: build the tree from all queries, then do one pass **bottom-up**: each node's top-k is the best k items among its own word (if a query ends there) and its children's top-k lists. That's a small merge per node, done once offline.

### 3. Ranking: which 10 make the cut

"Most searched" is a good start, but real systems blend several signals into a **score**:
- **Popularity**: how often the query was searched, and how often searching it led to a click or purchase. A query that leads to buying is worth more than one that leads to nothing.
- **Recency / trending**: counts are **time-decayed** so last week matters more than last year. A simple form is score = sum of searches x 0.5^(age in days / 7), so a search loses half its weight every 7 days. A new phone launch day can push "iphone 17" up within hours via a fast **trending** path.
- **Personalisation**: if you have been browsing running shoes, "nike" might suggest "nike running shoes" first for you. This is usually done by **re-ranking**: fetch a bigger candidate list (say top 30) from the shared trie, then reorder it per user using their recent history. The shared trie stays the same for everyone; only the small final step is personal.

### 4. Building it offline and refreshing it

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  L[Search and click logs] --> AG[Daily aggregation job]
  AG --> SC[Score and decay counts]
  SC --> FL[Remove blocked terms]
  FL --> BT[Build trie with top k]
  BT --> SN[Versioned snapshot]
  SN --> SV[Suggest servers load it]
  TR[Trending stream] --> SV
```

- A batch job (Spark or similar) runs every few hours or daily: aggregate logs into query -> count, apply decay and ranking, remove junk, build the trie, and write a **versioned snapshot** file.
- Suggestion servers **load the new snapshot into memory** and swap it in atomically: keep serving the old one until the new one is fully loaded, then switch a pointer.
- For freshness inside the day, a small **trending layer** (fed by a stream such as Kafka) counts the last few minutes or hours of searches and is merged with the trie results at request time.
- Why not update the trie live on every search? Writes on every keystroke from millions of users would fight with reads, and top-k lists all the way up the tree would need constant recomputation. **Read-heavy, slightly stale, rebuilt in batches** is the classic trade-off here, and users don't notice suggestions being a few hours old.

### 5. The client side: debounce and cache

A fast typist hits 5-8 keys per second. Sending a request for every key wastes server capacity and causes flicker.
- **Debouncing**: wait until the user pauses typing for about 50-150 ms before sending a request. Typing "iphone" quickly may send only 1-2 requests instead of 6.
- **Cancel stale requests**: if the answer for "ip" arrives after the answer for "iph", ignore it. Show only the response for the latest text.
- **Browser / app cache**: keep recent prefix -> suggestions in memory. Pressing backspace from "iph" to "ip" is served locally with zero network.
- **CDN cache**: the non-personalised response for a prefix is the same for everyone, so it can be cached at the CDN for a few minutes (a short **TTL**, time-to-live). Short prefixes like "i", "s", "sh" are requested millions of times; almost all of them never reach your servers.

### 6. Typo tolerance (briefly)

People type "ipone", "samsang", "sheos". Options, cheapest first:
- **Spelling-correction map** built from logs: if many people typed "ipone" and then immediately searched "iphone", map one to the other.
- **Edit distance**: allow 1 wrong, missing or extra letter, by exploring a few nearby branches of the trie.

### 7. Scaling out: sharding by prefix

One trie of the top tens of millions of queries may fit on one big server's memory, but traffic does not. So:
- **Replicate**: many identical copies behind a load balancer for read throughput.
- **Shard by prefix** when the data is too big: for example shard 1 holds a-f, shard 2 holds g-m, and so on. A request for "iph" goes to the shard owning "i".
- Letters are not evenly popular ("s" is huge, "x" is tiny), so split by **measured traffic**, not by alphabet, for example "sa-sh" on one shard, "si-sz" on another. Hot shards get more replicas.

### 8. Safety: filtering offensive terms

Suggestions are the brand speaking. Anything shown must be safe:
- A **blocklist** of offensive, adult, hateful or legally sensitive terms is applied **at build time** (so they never enter the trie) and again **at serve time** (so a newly added block works immediately, without waiting for the next rebuild).
- Guard against **manipulation**: bots searching a phrase repeatedly to force it into suggestions. Count unique users, not raw searches, and cap influence per user.

## A worked example

**A Flipkart-like app on a new iPhone launch day.**

1. Overnight, the batch job reads yesterday's logs: 900k searches for "iphone 15", 700k for "iphone 15 pro", 400k for "iphone cover", and so on. It applies the 7-day decay, drops queries with zero results and anything on the blocklist, builds the trie with top-10 lists at every node, and publishes snapshot v512. All suggestion servers load v512 and swap at 4 am.
2. At 10 am, Apple announces "iphone 17". Searches spike. The trending stream sees "iphone 17" jump from 0 to 50k searches in an hour. The trending layer starts mixing it into results for "iph", "ipho", "iphone" within minutes, long before the next nightly build.
3. Priya in Coimbatore opens the app and types "i", "p", "h" quickly. The app debounces: it waits 100 ms after "h" and sends one request: `GET /suggest?q=iph`.
4. The request hits the CDN. "iph" is a very hot prefix today, so the CDN already has a 60-second cached copy. Response in about 15 ms; no origin server touched.
5. Because Priya is logged in, a small personal step runs in the app: she viewed phone covers yesterday, so "iphone 15 cover" is nudged up from position 6 to 3. The base list came from the shared cache; only the reordering is personal.
6. She keeps typing "iphone 17 pr". This longer prefix isn't in the CDN cache, so the request goes to the shard owning "i", which walks 12 nodes and returns the stored top-10 in under 5 ms.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The server searches the product catalogue on every keystroke."** No. Suggestions come from precomputed lists of popular **queries**, not a live search over products. The full product search runs only when you press enter or tap a suggestion.
- **"A trie alone makes it fast."** A trie finds the prefix fast, but listing and sorting everything below it is slow. The speed comes from **storing top-k at each node**.
- **"Suggestions must be real-time fresh."** Hours-old data is fine for most queries. Use a small trending layer for the few that change fast, and keep the main trie batch-built.
- **"Personalisation means a separate trie per user."** That would be huge. Fetch shared candidates, then **re-rank per user** with a light model.
- **"Send a request for every key for best UX."** That increases load and causes flicker. **Debounce, cancel stale responses, cache**.
- **"Filtering happens once at build time."** Also filter at serve time so new blocks apply immediately.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Autocomplete is a read-heavy lookup, not a search. Offline, I aggregate search and click logs into query scores, using popularity, time decay for recency, and conversion. I build a trie, a prefix tree, and at every node I store the top k completions, so a request for 'iph' is just three steps down the tree and returning a ready list. That snapshot is versioned and loaded into memory on replicated suggestion servers, sharded by prefix based on traffic, and swapped atomically when a new build is ready. A small streaming layer adds trending queries between builds. On the client I debounce keystrokes by about 100 ms, drop stale responses and cache per prefix; the non-personal responses are cached on the CDN, so hot short prefixes rarely reach my servers. Personalisation is a re-rank of a slightly larger candidate list. Typos are handled with a correction map from logs and limited edit distance. And a blocklist runs at both build and serve time so nothing offensive is ever shown."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *How would you handle a sudden trend, like a launch?* A streaming counter over the last few minutes or hours, merged with the trie results at request time, plus a short CDN TTL so the change shows up quickly.
- *How much memory does it take?* Limit it to the top few million queries and cap prefix depth; store IDs instead of strings in the top-k lists. That typically fits in a few GB to tens of GB, which is fine in RAM, but measure it for your data.
- *Why not use a database `LIKE 'iph%'` query?* It scans and sorts at request time, which is too slow at tens of thousands of requests per second. Precomputed top-k gives constant-time answers.

## Key takeaways

- Suggestions are **precomputed**, not searched live.
- A **trie** finds a prefix in as many steps as letters typed.
- **Top-k stored at every node** makes lookups instant; the cost moves to offline build and memory.
- **Ranking** blends popularity, time-decayed recency, conversion and a light **personal re-rank**.
- Build **offline from logs**, publish **versioned snapshots**, swap atomically; add a small **trending** layer for freshness.
- On the client: **debounce**, drop stale responses, **cache per prefix**; cache shared responses on the **CDN**.
- Scale with **replicas** and **traffic-aware prefix sharding**.
- **Filter offensive terms** at build and serve time, and resist bot manipulation.

## Check yourself

1. Why is storing the top-k list at each trie node so important for speed?
   Answer: Without it, answering a short prefix like "i" means visiting and sorting every query below that node, possibly millions. With it, you walk one step per letter and return an already-ranked list, so the work per request is tiny.
2. Searches for a brand-new phone explode at 10 am but the trie is rebuilt nightly. How do suggestions catch up?
   Answer: A streaming trending layer counts recent searches and merges hot new queries into results at request time, and short CDN TTLs let the updated responses spread within minutes.
3. A user types "iphone" quickly. Without debouncing, how many requests may be sent, and with debouncing roughly how many?
   Answer: Up to 6, one per letter. With a 100 ms debounce, often just 1 or 2, sent when the user pauses, and stale responses for older prefixes are ignored.
4. Why split shards by measured traffic instead of evenly by alphabet?
   Answer: Letters are not equally popular. A shard holding all of "s" would get far more requests than one holding "x", so splitting by real load, and adding replicas to hot shards, keeps every server evenly busy.

question: Two people book the last train seat at the same moment. What is a database transaction, what does ACID really mean, and how do locks and isolation levels stop both of them getting the seat?
answer:
## The short answer

A **database transaction** is a group of database steps that the database treats as **one unit**: either **all** of them happen, or **none** of them do. If anything fails halfway, the database **rolls back** (undoes) the partial work.

**ACID** is the four promises a transaction gives you:
- **Atomicity**: all or nothing.
- **Consistency**: the data moves from one valid state to another valid state (rules like "seats can't go below zero" stay true).
- **Isolation**: transactions running at the same time don't trip over each other's half-finished work.
- **Durability**: once the database says "committed", the change survives a crash or power cut.

In the last-seat race, **atomicity alone does not save you**. Both people can read "1 seat left" and both can book. What stops it is **isolation**, enforced with **locks** or **version checks**. The three common fixes are:
1. **Lock the row before reading** (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), so the second person waits.
2. **Make the update itself conditional** (`UPDATE ... SET seats = seats - 1 WHERE seats > 0`) and check how many rows changed.
3. **Optimistic locking**: read a **version number**, and only update if the version hasn't changed; otherwise retry or fail.

**Isolation levels** (read committed, repeatable read, serializable) decide how strongly the database protects you by default. Higher levels catch more problems but cost more waiting or more retries.

## The intuition

Think of a **bank transfer** of 500 rupees from Asha to Ravi. Two steps: take 500 from Asha, add 500 to Ravi. If the server crashes after step one, 500 rupees has vanished. A transaction wraps both steps so the bank either does **both** or **neither**. That is the "all-or-nothing" idea.

Now the train. There is **one seat left** on a train. Asha and Ravi press "Book" in the same second. Each request does:
1. Read how many seats are left. (Both see **1**.)
2. If more than 0, create a booking and set seats to 0.

Both pass the check, both create a booking, both set seats to 0. Two tickets, one seat. Each request was "all or nothing", and still the result is wrong. The problem is not crashing midway; the problem is **two people looking at the same thing at the same time**.

Everyday fix: there is **one physical register** at the counter. Whoever picks up the pen first writes their name; the other person must **wait** until the pen is put down, and then sees the seat is gone. That pen is a **lock**.

Terms used below:
- **Commit**: make the transaction's changes permanent and visible.
- **Rollback**: throw away all of the transaction's changes.
- **Row lock**: a marker the database puts on a row so other transactions must wait before changing it (or, with some locks, reading it).
- **Race condition**: a bug where the result depends on who happens to run first.
- **Isolation level**: a setting that controls how much one transaction can see of others' in-progress or recently committed changes.
- **Deadlock**: two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds, so neither can move.

## How it actually works

### 1. A transaction in SQL

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 'asha';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 'ravi';
COMMIT;      -- both changes become visible together
-- if anything fails before COMMIT, the app runs ROLLBACK and nothing changed
```

How does the database keep these promises? For **atomicity and durability**, it writes changes to a **write-ahead log** (a log on disk written before the data pages). After a crash, it replays committed work and discards uncommitted work. For **isolation**, it uses **locks** and, in most modern databases, **MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control): each row keeps older versions, so readers can see a stable snapshot while writers create new versions.

### 2. ACID, one line each

| Letter | Plain meaning | Train example |
|---|---|---|
| **A**tomicity | All steps or none | Seat count drops and booking row is created, or neither happens |
| **C**onsistency | Rules stay true after every commit | A `CHECK (seats_left >= 0)` constraint is never broken |
| **I**solation | Concurrent transactions behave as if they ran more or less one by one | Asha and Ravi can't both take the last seat |
| **D**urability | Committed means saved, even after a crash | Asha's PNR still exists after the server reboots |


### 3. The race, step by step

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Asha
  participant DB as Database
  participant R as Ravi
  A->>DB: read seats left
  R->>DB: read seats left
  DB-->>A: 1
  DB-->>R: 1
  A->>DB: insert booking, set seats 0
  R->>DB: insert booking, set seats 0
  Note over DB: two bookings for one seat
```

This is a **check-then-act race**: someone slips in between the check and the act.

### 4. Fix 1: pessimistic locking with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

**Pessimistic** means "assume a clash will happen, so lock first".

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT seats_left FROM trains
 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND journey_date = '2026-10-20'
 FOR UPDATE;                         -- locks this row until COMMIT or ROLLBACK
-- app checks: seats_left > 0 ?
UPDATE trains SET seats_left = seats_left - 1
 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND journey_date = '2026-10-20';
INSERT INTO bookings (train_id, journey_date, user_id) VALUES (12635, '2026-10-20', 'asha');
COMMIT;
```

Asha's `FOR UPDATE` takes a **row lock**. Ravi's `FOR UPDATE` on the same row **waits**. When Asha commits, Ravi's query continues and reads the fresh value **0**, so his app says "sold out". Correct.

Trade-off: everyone wanting that row forms a **queue**. Fine for one train; painful if thousands of people hammer one hot row. Keep the transaction **short** (no network calls to a payment gateway while holding the lock).

### 5. Fix 2: a conditional update (atomic check-and-act)

Put the check **inside** the update, so the database does check and act as one step on a locked row:

```sql
UPDATE trains
   SET seats_left = seats_left - 1
 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND journey_date = '2026-10-20'
   AND seats_left > 0;
-- rows affected = 1  -> you got the seat, now insert the booking in the same transaction
-- rows affected = 0  -> sold out
```

The `UPDATE` locks the row while it runs. If Ravi's update arrives while Asha's transaction is still open, it waits; once Asha commits, the database re-checks the row, sees `seats_left = 0`, and Ravi's update changes **0 rows**. This is usually the **simplest and fastest** fix for counters like stock and seats. Add a `CHECK (seats_left >= 0)` constraint as a safety net.

### 6. Fix 3: optimistic locking with a version column

**Optimistic** means "assume clashes are rare; don't lock, but detect a clash at write time".

```sql
-- read, no lock
SELECT seats_left, version FROM trains WHERE train_id = 12635;   -- 1, version 7

-- write only if nobody changed it since
UPDATE trains SET seats_left = 0, version = 8
 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND version = 7;
-- 1 row -> success. 0 rows -> someone else changed it: re-read and retry, or report sold out
```

In Java with JPA/Hibernate you get this by adding a field annotated `@Version`; a clash throws `OptimisticLockException`:

```java
@Entity
class Train {
    @Id Long id;
    int seatsLeft;
    @Version long version;   // Hibernate adds "AND version = ?" to every update
}
```

Good when clashes are **rare** and you don't want readers to block (for example, editing a user profile). Bad for a **hot** row like the last seats in a festive rush: most attempts fail and retry, wasting work.

### 7. Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent

An **anomaly** is a weird result caused by concurrent transactions. The three to know:
- **Dirty read**: you read data another transaction has **not committed yet**, and it later rolls back. You acted on something that never really existed.
- **Non-repeatable read**: you read a row twice in the same transaction and get **different values**, because someone committed a change in between.
- **Lost update**: two transactions read the same value, both write based on it, and one write **silently overwrites** the other (our train race).

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Lost update |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read committed | Prevented | Possible | Possible |
| Repeatable read | Prevented | Prevented | Depends on database |
| Serializable | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

- **Read committed**: each statement sees only committed data, as of that statement. **PostgreSQL's default.**
- **Repeatable read**: the whole transaction sees one **snapshot** taken at its first read. **MySQL InnoDB's default.** In PostgreSQL, if two repeatable-read transactions update the same row, the second gets a **serialization error** and must retry, so the lost update is caught. In MySQL InnoDB, a plain read-then-write can still lose an update unless you use `FOR UPDATE` or a conditional update.
- **Serializable**: the result must be the same as if transactions ran **one at a time**. The database blocks or aborts transactions that would break this. Safest, but more aborts and retries under load.

So the answer to "which isolation level fixes the train race?" is: **serializable always does; lower levels need an explicit lock or a conditional update.** Most teams stay at read committed and use Fix 1 or Fix 2 on the specific hot path.

### 8. Deadlocks, briefly

Transaction 1 locks seat row A then wants row B; transaction 2 locks B then wants A. Each waits for the other forever. Databases detect this and **abort one** with a deadlock error; your code should **retry** it. To avoid deadlocks: **always lock rows in the same order** (for example, by seat ID ascending), keep transactions short, and don't hold locks while calling slow external services.

## A worked example

**A Diwali-week train booking flow in an IRCTC-like system** (illustrative design, not any real company's internals).

1. Train 12635, sleeper class, has **3 seats left**. At 10:00:00, **5 users** tap "Book" within 200 ms.
2. Each request opens a transaction and runs the **conditional update**: `UPDATE inventory SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND class = 'SL' AND seats_left > 0`.
3. The database applies them one at a time on that row. Users 1, 2 and 3 each get **1 row affected**; users 4 and 5 get **0 rows**. Seats left: 3, 2, 1, 0.
4. Users 1-3, in the **same transaction**, insert a `bookings` row with status `PENDING_PAYMENT` and a 10-minute hold. **Commit.** The lock was held for a few milliseconds, never during payment.
5. Users 4-5 are told "Waitlisted" and get a waitlist entry instead.
6. User 2's UPI payment fails. A cleanup job, in one transaction, marks booking 2 as `EXPIRED` **and** adds 1 back to `seats_left`. Atomicity matters here: doing only one of those two steps would leak or invent a seat.
7. That freed seat goes to the first waitlisted user, again via a conditional update, so even if two cleanup workers run at once, the seat is handed out only once.
8. The server crashes at 10:00:05. On restart, **durability** means the three committed bookings are still there; any half-done transaction is rolled back.


## Common misconceptions

- **"Wrapping code in a transaction makes it safe from races."** Atomicity protects against **partial** failure, not against **concurrent** readers. At read committed, two transactions can still both see 1 seat. You need a lock, a conditional update, or serializable isolation.
- **"Serializable is too slow, so never use it."** It costs retries under contention, but for a small, critical piece of logic it can be the simplest correct option. It depends on the database and the load; measure.
- **"Optimistic locking is always faster."** Only when clashes are rare. On a hot row, most attempts fail and retry, which is slower than just queueing on a lock.
- **"Repeatable read means the same thing everywhere."** PostgreSQL and MySQL behave differently on concurrent updates. Know your database's actual rules.
- **"Consistency in ACID is the same as consistency in CAP."** ACID's C means your **data rules** hold. CAP's C means all replicas return the **latest value**. Different ideas, same word.

## How to say it in an interview

*"A transaction is a group of database operations that succeed or fail as one unit, like a bank transfer where the debit and credit must both happen or neither. ACID is the set of guarantees: atomicity is all-or-nothing, consistency means declared rules like seats never going negative always hold, isolation means concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work, and durability means a commit survives a crash. For the last-seat race, atomicity isn't enough: both users can read one seat left. The simplest fix is a conditional update, UPDATE seats minus one WHERE seats greater than zero, and check the affected row count. Alternatives are SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock the row first, or optimistic locking with a version column when clashes are rare. Isolation levels set the default protection: read committed stops dirty reads, repeatable read gives a stable snapshot, and serializable makes it behave as if transactions ran one by one, at the cost of more retries. I keep locked sections short, lock rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks, and retry on deadlock or serialization errors."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *When would you pick pessimistic over optimistic locking?* Pessimistic when clashes are frequent (a hot row like flash-sale stock), because waiting in a queue beats repeated failed retries. Optimistic when clashes are rare and you don't want reads to block.
- *What happens if payment takes 30 seconds?* Never hold a database lock during it. Reserve the seat with a short transaction (status `HELD` with an expiry), commit, take payment, then confirm or release in another short transaction.
- *How would this work across multiple databases or services?* A single local transaction can't span them. You'd use a saga (a chain of local transactions with compensating undo steps) or reserve-then-confirm patterns, and make each step idempotent.

## Key takeaways

- A **transaction** groups steps into **all-or-nothing**; commit makes them permanent, rollback undoes them.
- **ACID**: atomicity (all or none), consistency (declared rules hold), isolation (no stepping on each other), durability (commits survive crashes).
- Atomicity does **not** stop races; the last-seat bug is an **isolation** problem.
- Three practical fixes: **conditional update** (`WHERE seats > 0`), **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`**, **optimistic version column**.
- Isolation levels trade safety for throughput; **behaviour of repeatable read differs between PostgreSQL and MySQL**.
- Know the anomalies: **dirty read, non-repeatable read, lost update**.
- **Deadlocks** happen; lock in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and retry.

## Check yourself

1. Two requests both run `SELECT seats_left` (get 1) and then `UPDATE trains SET seats_left = 0` inside separate transactions at read committed. Is the race prevented? Why or why not?
   Answer: No. Each transaction is atomic, but read committed lets both read 1 before either writes, so both book. You need FOR UPDATE, a conditional update, or a stricter isolation level.
2. Your conditional update `... WHERE seats_left > 0` returns 0 rows affected. What does that mean, and what should the app do?
   Answer: Someone else took the last seat (or there were none). The app should not insert a booking; it should roll back or simply report sold out or offer the waitlist.
3. A flash sale has 100 units and 50,000 buyers in one minute. Would you choose optimistic locking with a version column? Explain.
   Answer: Usually not. With so many clashes on one row, most optimistic attempts fail and retry, wasting work. A conditional decrement or a short pessimistic lock queues requests and is more efficient here.
4. Transaction 1 locks seat 5 then seat 6; transaction 2 locks seat 6 then seat 5. What can happen, and how do you prevent it?
   Answer: A deadlock: each waits for the other, and the database aborts one. Prevent it by always locking seats in the same order, such as ascending seat ID, keeping transactions short, and retrying the aborted one.

question: What are database replication and sharding, what problem does each solve, and how do you know when you need them?
answer:
## The short answer

When one database server can no longer keep up, you have two classic tools.

- **Replication** means keeping **copies** of the same data on several servers. One server, the **primary**, accepts writes. The others, the **replicas**, copy every change and serve reads. It solves two problems: **too many reads** for one machine, and **the machine dying** (a replica can take over, which is called **failover**). It does **not** help if you have too many writes or too much data, because every copy still holds everything and applies every write.
- **Sharding** means **splitting** the data into pieces, called **shards**, and putting each piece on a different server. Shard 1 holds some users, shard 2 holds others. It solves **too much data** and **too many writes** for one machine. The price is complexity: you must pick a **shard key**, queries that touch many shards get slow, and moving data between shards later is painful.

When do you need them? Measure first, and try **vertical scaling** (a bigger machine), indexes and caching before either. Add **replicas** when reads dominate or downtime is unacceptable. **Shard** only when writes or data size will soon exceed the biggest sensible machine.

## The intuition

Think of a town **library** with one librarian and one building.

As the town grows, two different things can go wrong:

1. **Too many people want to read.** The queue at the desk is long, but the books themselves fit fine. The fix: open **branch libraries** that hold **photocopies** of every book. Readers go to any branch. New books still arrive at the main library first, and the branches get copies a little later. That is **replication**. The main library is the **primary**; the branches are **read replicas**. If the main library burns down, one branch can be promoted to be the new main one (**failover**). The catch: a book that arrived this morning may not be at the branch yet. That delay is **replication lag**.
2. **Too many books for one building**, and too many new books arriving every day for one person to shelve. Photocopies do not help, because every branch would still need every book. The fix: **split the collection**. Building A holds authors A to H, building B holds I to P, building C holds Q to Z. That is **sharding**. The rule "which building holds which book" is the **shard key** (here, the author's surname). Now each building is smaller and each librarian shelves only a third of the new books. But a question like "list all books published in 2024" means visiting all three buildings, which is a **cross-shard query**.

Terms used below:

- **Vertical scaling (scale up)**: buying a bigger machine, more CPU, RAM, faster disk.
- **Horizontal scaling (scale out)**: adding more machines.
- **QPS**: queries per second.
- **Primary / replica**: the server that takes writes, and the servers that copy it.
- **Shard**: one piece of a split dataset, living on its own server (often with its own replicas).
- **Shard key**: the column used to decide which shard a row belongs to.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why one machine runs out

A single database (MySQL, PostgreSQL) is limited by **CPU**, **RAM** (holding hot data and indexes), **disk I/O** and **disk size**. A modest server might handle 2,000 simple queries per second; a 64-core, 512 GB machine perhaps 30,000 to 50,000, depending heavily on the queries. Writes cost more than reads because each one updates indexes and the log. When the **working set** (the data touched often) no longer fits in RAM, performance drops sharply because queries hit disk.

### 2. Vertical scaling comes first

Before replication or sharding, do the cheap things:

- Add the **right indexes** and fix slow queries. One missing index can cost 10x.
- Add a **cache** (Redis) for hot reads like product pages.
- Buy a **bigger machine**. It is boring, but it needs no code change.

It has a ceiling and gets expensive near the top, but many systems never need more.

### 3. Replication: copies of everything

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  App[App servers] -->|writes| P[Primary DB]
  App -->|reads| R1[Replica 1]
  App -->|reads| R2[Replica 2]
  P -->|change log| R1
  P -->|change log| R2
  P -.->|if primary dies| F[Promote a replica]
```

How it works: the primary records every change in a log (the **binlog** in MySQL, the **WAL** or write-ahead log in PostgreSQL). Replicas stream that log and replay it, so they end up with the same data.

- **Read scaling**: if traffic is 90% reads, one primary plus four replicas can serve roughly five times the reads. Writes do **not** scale: every replica still replays every write.
- **Failover**: if the primary dies, a replica is promoted. Tools or managed services (for example a cloud managed database) do this in seconds to a minute or two.
- **Asynchronous vs synchronous**: with **async** replication, the primary confirms the write before replicas have it. It is fast, but if the primary dies, the last few writes may be lost. With **sync** (or semi-sync) replication, the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm. It is safer but each write is slower. Most systems use async or semi-sync, a context-dependent choice.

**Replication lag** is the delay between a write on the primary and its appearance on a replica. Usually milliseconds, but under heavy load it can grow to seconds or minutes. This causes the classic bug, the **read-your-own-writes** problem: a user changes their address (write to primary), the page reloads (read from a replica), and the old address shows. Fixes:

- Read from the **primary** for a few seconds after that user writes.
- Always read the user's **own** critical data (cart, latest order) from the primary.
- Only use a replica that has caught up to the user's last write position.

```java
// Route a read: primary if this user wrote recently, else a replica
DataSource pick(long userId) {
    Long last = lastWriteAt.get(userId);           // set on every write
    boolean recent = last != null && System.currentTimeMillis() - last < 5_000;
    return recent ? primary : replicas.next();      // round-robin replicas
}
```

### 4. Sharding: splitting the data

With sharding, each shard holds a **subset of rows** and handles only the writes for those rows. Four shards means roughly a quarter of the data and writes each. Each shard is usually itself a primary with replicas.

**Choosing the shard key** is the most important decision. A good key:

- **spreads load evenly** across shards,
- matches **how you query**, so most queries hit one shard,
- **does not change** for a row.

For an orders database, compare:

| Shard key | Even spread? | Common queries on one shard? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `user_id` | Yes, millions of users | "My orders" hits one shard | Usually good |
| `city` | No, Bengaluru dwarfs a small town | City reports yes, user history no | Hot shards |
| `order_id` | Yes | Lookup by order id yes, "my orders" no | Fine only with a lookup index |

**Range sharding** assigns key ranges: users 1 to 10 million on shard 1, 10 to 20 million on shard 2. Range scans are easy, but new users all land on the latest shard, so it gets hot. **Hash sharding** computes `hash(user_id) % N` and spreads keys evenly, but range queries must ask every shard. Many systems use **consistent hashing** or a fixed large number of **virtual shards** (say 1,024 logical buckets mapped onto 8 servers) so that adding servers only moves some buckets, not everything.

**Hot shards** happen when one key gets huge traffic: a celebrity seller, or a single flash-sale product. Hashing on user does not help if one seller has a million orders a minute. Fixes include splitting that key further, caching, or queueing writes.

**Cross-shard queries and joins** are the main pain. "Total sales across India today" must ask every shard and merge (**scatter-gather**). A join between orders (sharded by user) and sellers (sharded by seller) cannot be done inside one database. A transaction touching two shards needs extra machinery (sagas or two-phase commit). Teams **denormalise** (copy needed fields), keep a **separate index** keyed differently, or use a warehouse for analytics.

**Resharding** is moving data when you add shards. With naive `hash % 4` going to `hash % 8`, about half the rows must move. It means copying live data, catching up on new writes, switching traffic, and verifying, all without downtime. Planning many virtual shards up front makes this far easier. Tools like **Vitess** (MySQL) or **Citus** (PostgreSQL) automate much of this.

### 5. How to know when you need which

| Symptom you measure | Likely next step |
|---|---|
| Slow queries, CPU spikes from a few queries | Indexes, query fixes |
| Read QPS high, primary CPU mostly reads | Cache, then read replicas |
| Any downtime is unacceptable | At least one replica with failover |
| Write QPS near primary limit | Batch writes, bigger box, then shard |
| Data size heading past a few TB, backups take hours | Archive old data, then shard |

## A worked example

**An orders database at a Flipkart-like marketplace**, numbers simplified.

**Year 1.** 20,000 orders a day. One PostgreSQL server (8 cores, 32 GB). Peak 300 QPS, CPU at 15%. Sharding would be pure cost.

**Year 2.** 300,000 orders a day; peak 6,000 QPS. Tracking pages hammer the database and CPU hits 85% in the evening. The team checks: 90% of queries are reads. Fixes in order: add a missing index on `(user_id, created_at)` (CPU drops to 60%), cache tracking status in Redis for 30 seconds, then **upgrade** to 32 cores and 256 GB RAM. Also add **two async read replicas**, mainly so a failed primary does not mean an outage.

First bug: a customer cancels, and "My orders" still shows "Placed", read from a replica 800 ms behind. Fix: after a write, that user reads from the primary for 5 seconds.

**Year 4, before the festive sale.** 3 million orders on a normal day, 25 million on sale day. Peak writes forecast at 15,000 per second, with 4 TB of order data growing 2 TB a year. Replicas do not help writes; every replica would replay all 15,000 writes per second. The biggest machine available tops out well below the forecast for this write pattern. Now **sharding** is justified.

- **Shard key: `user_id`.** "My orders", cancellations and returns are per user, so they hit one shard. `city` was rejected: Bengaluru, Delhi and Mumbai would be hot.
- **1,024 virtual shards** mapped to **8 physical shards**, each with a primary and two replicas. About 1,900 peak writes per second and 500 GB per shard, comfortable headroom.
- A small **routing layer** maps `user_id` to virtual shard to server.
- **Seller dashboards** need "all orders for seller S", which is cross-shard. Solution: every order event is published to a stream and a separate **seller-orders store**, keyed by seller, is built from it. Seconds of delay are acceptable there.
- **Order ID lookup** from customer care: the order ID encodes the virtual shard number, so it routes directly.

**Year 6.** 8 shards become 16. Thanks to virtual shards, the team moves 512 buckets one at a time (copy, stream changes, brief pause, flip routing, verify): weeks of careful work, no customer-visible downtime.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Replicas scale writes."** They do not. Every replica applies every write. Replicas scale reads and give failover.
- **"Replication is a backup."** If someone runs `DELETE FROM orders` by mistake, replicas delete it too, within milliseconds. You still need real backups and point-in-time recovery.
- **"Shard early so we never have to later."** Sharding adds permanent complexity to every query, migration and report. Most systems should scale up, cache and replicate first, and shard only when numbers show it is coming. (Designing a clean key like `user_id` early is cheap and wise; actually splitting is not.)
- **"Any column with many values is a good shard key."** It also must match your main queries and spread load. `city` has many values but terrible skew.
- **"Hash sharding removes hot spots."** It spreads different keys evenly, but one very hot key (a mega-seller, a flash-sale item) still lands on one shard.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Replication and sharding solve different limits of a single database. Replication keeps full copies of the data: one primary takes writes and replicas stream its log and serve reads. That scales reads and gives failover if the primary dies, but it doesn't scale writes, and because replication is usually asynchronous there's lag, so I make sure users read their own recent writes from the primary. Sharding splits the data across servers by a shard key, so each server holds and writes only part of it. That scales writes and storage. The hard part is the key: for orders I'd use user ID, because it spreads evenly and most queries are per user, rather than city, which creates hot shards. The costs are cross-shard queries and joins, and resharding later, so I'd use many virtual shards from the start. In order, I'd fix queries and add caching, scale up, add replicas, and only shard when write rate or data size is clearly heading past one machine."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *How would you query across shards, say all orders for a seller?* Avoid it on the hot path: build a separate store keyed by seller from an event stream, or use scatter-gather for rare queries and a warehouse for reports.
- *What happens to in-flight writes during failover?* With async replication, the last few writes may not have reached the new primary and can be lost. Semi-sync replication reduces this at the cost of write latency; idempotent retries from clients help recover.
- *How would you add shards without downtime?* Pre-split into many virtual shards, then move buckets one at a time: bulk copy, stream changes to catch up, short write pause, flip routing, verify.

## Key takeaways

- **Replication = copies**; it scales **reads** and gives **failover**, not write capacity.
- **Sharding = splitting**; it scales **writes and data size**, at the cost of complexity.
- **Replication lag** is real; handle **read-your-own-writes** by routing recent writers to the primary.
- The **shard key** decides everything: even spread, matches main queries, never changes. `user_id` beats `city` for orders.
- **Range** sharding helps scans but creates hot ranges; **hash** sharding spreads evenly but scatters range queries.
- **Cross-shard joins** and **resharding** are the main ongoing costs; plan virtual shards early.
- **Scale up, index and cache first**; shard when measurements, not fear, say so.
- Replicas are **not backups**.

## Check yourself

1. Your read replicas are at 20% CPU but the primary is at 95%, and almost all of its load is INSERT and UPDATE. Will adding two more replicas help?
   Answer: No. Replicas only take reads, and each one still replays every write. You need to reduce or spread writes: batching, a bigger primary, or eventually sharding.
2. A user updates their phone number, and the profile page immediately shows the old number. What is happening and how do you fix it?
   Answer: The read went to a replica that had not yet applied the write (replication lag). Route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write, or wait for the replica to reach the write's log position.
3. Why is `city` a poor shard key for an orders table in India?
   Answer: Traffic is very uneven, so metros like Bengaluru or Mumbai would become hot shards, and per-user queries like order history would not map to a single shard if a user orders across cities.
4. You sharded with `hash(user_id) % 4` and now need 8 servers. Why is this painful and what would have made it easier?
   Answer: Changing the modulus moves about half of all rows, which must be copied live without downtime. Starting with many virtual shards (for example 1,024 buckets mapped onto servers) means you move whole buckets, only as many as needed, and update a routing map.

question: How does a load balancer decide which server gets your request, and what happens when one of those servers dies mid-traffic?
answer:
## The short answer

A **load balancer** is a traffic cop that sits in front of a group of identical servers (a **pool**). Every request hits the load balancer first, and it picks one healthy server to send it to.

- **How it picks:** it uses a simple rule called an **algorithm**. The common ones are **round robin** (take turns), **weighted round robin** (bigger servers get more turns), **least connections** (send to the least busy one) and **consistent hashing** (the same user or key always goes to the same server).
- **How it knows a server is dead:** **health checks**. It pings each server every few seconds (**active**), and it watches real requests for errors and timeouts (**passive**). After a few failures in a row, the server is taken out of the pool.
- **What happens mid-traffic:** new requests stop going to the dead server within seconds. Requests *already inside* it usually fail and are **retried** on another server, which is only safe if the request is **idempotent** (doing it twice has the same effect as once).

## The intuition

Think of a **toll plaza** on a highway with 10 booths.

- Cars are **requests**. Booths are **servers**. The person in the tower directing cars to lanes is the **load balancer**.
- The simplest rule is "next car goes to the next booth": booth 1, 2, 3 ... 10, then back to 1. That is **round robin**.
- Some booths have two operators and work twice as fast. You send them twice as many cars. That is **weighted round robin**.
- If a truck is stuck paying in coins, send the next car to the **shortest queue**. That is **least connections**.
- Regular commuters with a monthly pass always use booth 4, because booth 4 has their pass on file. That is **stickiness** (via hashing or cookies).
- The director radios each booth: "Are you open?" Three silences and it is coned off. That is an **active health check**. Noticing cars stuck at one booth is a **passive health check**.
- Before a shift change, no new cars go to a booth, but cars in its lane finish. That is **connection draining**.
- If the director faints, the plaza jams, so a **second director** stands ready. That is a **high-availability pair**.

Terms used below:
- **Health check:** a regular test that a server is alive and able to serve.
- **Idempotent:** safe to repeat. Reading a product page is idempotent. "Charge Rs 500" is not, unless you add an idempotency key.
- **Stateless server:** a server that keeps no user data in its own memory between requests. Session data lives in a shared store like Redis.

## How it actually works

### 1. Where the load balancer sits

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U[Users] --> D[DNS or anycast IP]
  D --> L1[Load balancer A]
  D --> L2[Load balancer B standby]
  L1 --> S1[Server 1]
  L1 --> S2[Server 2]
  L1 --> S3[Server 3 dead]
  L2 -.-> S1
  S1 --> R[Shared Redis and DB]
  S2 --> R
```

The phone resolves the domain to the load balancer's IP and connects; the load balancer forwards to a pool server. Server 3 failed its health checks, so it gets nothing. Sessions live in shared Redis, not server memory.

### 2. Layer 4 vs Layer 7

"Layer" comes from the networking model. The difference is **how much of the request the load balancer reads**.

| | **L4 (transport)** | **L7 (application)** |
|---|---|---|
| Looks at | IP address and port (TCP/UDP) | Full HTTP request: URL, headers, cookies |
| Can route by | Connection only | Path, host, header, cookie |
| Example rule | All TCP on port 443 to pool A | `/search` to search pool, `/cart` to cart pool |
| TLS (HTTPS) | Usually passed through | Usually ended here (TLS termination) |
| Examples | AWS NLB, Linux IPVS | NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy in HTTP mode, AWS ALB |

A common setup is **both**: L4 at the edge spreads connections across a fleet of L7 proxies, which do the smart routing. L4 is faster; L7 is smarter.

### 3. The algorithms, with small examples

**Round robin.** Servers A, B, C. Requests 1 to 6 go A, B, C, A, B, C. Simple and fair if every server is the same and every request costs about the same.

**Weighted round robin.** A has 8 CPUs, B and C have 4. Give weights 2, 1, 1. Out of every 4 requests, A gets 2, B gets 1, C gets 1. Also used for **canary releases**: give a new version weight 1 and the old version weight 99, so 1% of traffic tries the new code.

**Least connections.** A has 12 open requests, B has 3, C has 7. The next request goes to B. Better when requests vary a lot (a quick product page vs a slow invoice PDF). A cheap cousin, **power of two choices**, picks 2 servers at random and uses the less busy one.

**Consistent hashing (for stickiness).** Hash a key, such as user ID or cart ID, to pick a server, so the same key always lands on the same server. Plain `hash(key) % N` has a problem: if N changes from 3 to 4, almost every key moves. **Consistent hashing** places servers on a ring and each key goes to the next server clockwise. Adding or removing one server moves only about **1/N of keys**.

```java
// Tiny consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes
import java.util.*;

class HashRing {
    private final TreeMap<Integer, String> ring = new TreeMap<>();
    private static final int VNODES = 100;   // spreads each server around the ring

    void add(String server) {
        for (int i = 0; i < VNODES; i++) ring.put((server + "#" + i).hashCode(), server);
    }
    void remove(String server) {
        for (int i = 0; i < VNODES; i++) ring.remove((server + "#" + i).hashCode());
    }
    String pick(String key) {
        Map.Entry<Integer, String> e = ring.ceilingEntry(key.hashCode());
        return (e != null ? e : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();   // wrap around
    }
}
```

(Real systems use a better hash, such as MurmurHash.) Hashing helps when a server holds a **local cache** per key, keeping it warm.

### 4. Health checks and removing dead servers

**Active checks:** every few seconds the load balancer calls something like `GET /health` on each server.

```
health_check:
  path: /health
  interval: 5s
  timeout: 2s
  unhealthy_threshold: 3   # 3 failures in a row -> remove
  healthy_threshold: 2     # 2 passes in a row -> add back
```

A dead server is removed in about **10 to 15 seconds**. Shorter intervals detect faster but can flap on brief hiccups.

**Passive checks (outlier detection):** the load balancer watches real traffic. If server C returns 5 errors or timeouts in a row, it is **ejected** for, say, 30 seconds, even before the next active check. This catches a server that answers `/health` fine but fails real requests.

**Keep `/health` shallow.** If it fails whenever the shared database is slow, *every* server fails at once and the whole pool is removed. Many load balancers **fail open**: if all look unhealthy, send to all anyway.

**When a server dies mid-traffic:**
1. Requests already sent to it get a connection reset or time out.
2. The load balancer can **retry** them on another server, but only for safe (idempotent) requests like GET. Retrying a POST "place order" could create a duplicate order unless the API uses an **idempotency key**.
3. Passive checks eject it within seconds; active checks confirm it.
4. The remaining servers absorb the load, so keep **spare capacity** (headroom).

### 5. Connection draining for deploys

Deploys remove servers on purpose. **Connection draining** means:
1. Mark the server as "draining". The load balancer sends it **no new requests**.
2. Requests already in progress are allowed to finish, up to a timeout like 30 to 60 seconds.
3. Then the server is stopped and replaced.

The app must help: on SIGTERM (the shutdown signal), fail `/health`, finish in-flight work, then exit. Without draining, every deploy causes an error burst.

### 6. Sticky sessions, and why stateless is better

**Sticky sessions** send a user to the same server every time, usually via a load balancer cookie, because the server keeps their session **in its own memory**.

Problems:
- If that server dies, the cart or login is **lost**.
- Load becomes **uneven**, and new autoscaled servers get only new users.

Better: **stateless servers**, with session data in Redis or a signed token (like a JWT). Any server can serve any request. Stickiness is fine as a **performance hint** (warm cache), never for correctness.

### 7. The load balancer as a single point of failure

If you have one load balancer and it dies, the whole site is down, no matter how many servers you have. Fixes, usually combined:
- **Active-passive pair:** two load balancers share a **virtual IP**. The standby watches a heartbeat and takes over the IP within seconds.
- **DNS with several IPs:** clients spread across many load balancers. Weakness: DNS answers are **cached**, so removing a dead IP can take minutes (depends on the TTL, time to live).
- **Anycast:** the **same IP** is announced from many sites via BGP (internet routing). Users reach the nearest healthy site; if one fails, routers shift to the next. CDNs and cloud load balancers work this way.

### 8. Autoscaling interplay

**Autoscaling** adds or removes servers based on load (CPU, requests per second):
- A new server starts, registers in the pool, and receives traffic only after it **passes health checks**. Give it a **warm-up** period (slow start) so a cold server with an empty cache is not flooded instantly.
- When scaling in, the server is **drained** first, then terminated.
- Scaling takes **minutes**; failures take **seconds**. For known spikes like a midnight sale, **pre-scale**.

## A worked example

**The midnight opening of a big festive sale on a Flipkart-like marketplace.**

1. **Before the sale:** the product service normally runs 40 servers. The team pre-scales to 200 an hour early, since autoscaling cannot add 160 servers in 30 seconds. Traffic arrives on an **anycast IP** at L4 load balancers, which feed L7 proxies.
2. **Routing:** L7 proxies send `/search`, `/product` and `/checkout` to separate pools, each using **least connections**, because some product pages are much slower than others.
3. **Stateless:** cart and session live in Redis, so one request can hit server 17 and the next server 112.
4. **00:03, server 57 runs out of memory and crashes.** In-flight requests fail; the proxy retries the GETs elsewhere, so users see a slightly slower page. Passive detection ejects it in about 2 seconds; active checks confirm at 15.
5. **Load shifts:** 199 servers carry the load of 200, 0.5% more each. With 30% headroom, nobody notices.
6. **Checkout is different:** a "place order" POST that was inside server 57 when it died is **not** automatically retried by the proxy. The app retries it with the same **idempotency key**, so the order service recognises the duplicate and does not create two orders or charge twice.
7. **The autoscaler** sees the pool one server short and starts a replacement. It joins after passing 2 health checks, with a 60-second slow start.
8. **01:00 hotfix:** servers are replaced 10% at a time with 30-second **draining**; errors stay flat.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Round robin spreads load evenly."** It spreads *requests* evenly, not *work*. If some requests take 10 ms and others 2 s, one server can be overloaded. Least connections or power of two choices handle this better.
- **"When a server dies, the load balancer saves every request."** Requests already inside that server usually fail. Only safe, idempotent requests can be retried automatically. Non-idempotent ones need idempotency keys.
- **"A 200 from /health means the server is fine."** It only proves the process is up; real calls can still fail, which is why passive checks matter.
- **"Sticky sessions are needed for logged-in users."** Only if sessions live in server memory. Move them to Redis.
- **"Adding a load balancer makes the system highly available."** A single load balancer is a new single point of failure. You need a pair, multiple instances behind DNS or anycast, or a managed multi-zone service.

## How to say it in an interview

*"A load balancer sits in front of a pool of identical servers and picks one per request. At layer 4 it sees only IPs and ports, so it is fast; at layer 7 it reads HTTP, so it can route by path or header. It picks using round robin for equal servers, weighted for different sizes or canaries, least connections when request costs vary, and consistent hashing when the same key should hit the same server. It detects dead servers with active health checks, say every 5 seconds and out after 3 failures, plus passive checks on real errors. When a server dies mid-traffic, new requests stop within seconds; in-flight ones fail and are retried elsewhere only if idempotent, so writes need idempotency keys. Deploys use connection draining. Servers stay stateless, sessions in Redis. And the load balancer itself must be redundant: an HA pair, DNS, or anycast."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *Why consistent hashing instead of hash mod N?* With mod N, changing the number of servers remaps almost every key, so every cache goes cold at once. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys when a server is added or removed.
- *How fast should health checks detect failure?* Faster means fewer failed requests but more false removals. About 10 to 15 seconds active, plus passive ejection in a second or two, is common.
- *What if all servers fail health checks at once?* That usually means a shared dependency or a bad health check, not dead servers. Many load balancers fail open and keep sending traffic; the fix is shallow health checks plus separate alerting on dependencies.

## Key takeaways

- A load balancer picks **one healthy server per request** from a pool, using an **algorithm**.
- **L4** routes by IP and port (fast); **L7** reads HTTP and routes by path, host or cookie (smart).
- **Round robin** for equal work, **weighted** for unequal servers or canaries, **least connections** for uneven requests, **consistent hashing** for key affinity.
- **Active plus passive health checks** remove dead servers in seconds; keep the health endpoint shallow.
- Mid-traffic failures hurt **in-flight requests**; retry only **idempotent** ones, and use **idempotency keys** for writes.
- **Connection draining** makes deploys and scale-in error-free.
- Prefer **stateless servers**; sticky sessions make failures and scaling worse.
- The load balancer must be **redundant** (HA pair, DNS, anycast), and **pre-scale** for known spikes because autoscaling is slow.

## Check yourself

1. Servers A, B and C use round robin. Every third request is a slow 3-second report, and it always lands on C. What goes wrong, and what algorithm fixes it?
   Answer: C builds a queue while A and B idle, because round robin counts requests, not work. Least connections sends new requests to the server with fewer in progress.
2. You have 4 cache servers and use hash(userId) % 4. You add a 5th server. What happens to the cache hit rate, and how does consistent hashing help?
   Answer: About 80% of keys move to a different server, so most caches go cold and the database gets hit hard. With consistent hashing only about 1/5 of keys move, so most of the cache stays warm.
3. A server crashes while handling a "place order" POST. Should the load balancer retry it on another server automatically?
   Answer: Not blindly: the order may already exist, so a retry could duplicate it. Retry only with an idempotency key the order service checks.
4. Your site has 50 servers but one load balancer, and that load balancer's machine fails. What happens, and name two ways to prevent it?
   Answer: The whole site goes down, because every request passes through that one machine. Prevent it with an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, several load balancers behind DNS, anycast, or a managed multi-zone cloud load balancer.

question: What does the CAP theorem really say, in plain words, and how does it change real design choices like a bank balance versus a like count?
answer:
## The short answer

The **CAP theorem** says: when your data is copied across several machines and the **network between them breaks**, each machine has to choose between two things. It can **stay correct** (refuse to answer, or wait, until it can be sure its data is up to date), or it can **stay available** (answer right away, even if the answer might be stale or might conflict with another machine). It cannot do both at that moment.

In letters:
- **C (Consistency)**: every read sees the latest write, as if there were only one copy.
- **A (Availability)**: every request to a working machine gets a real answer, not an error.
- **P (Partition tolerance)**: the system keeps running even when messages between machines are lost.

Networks *do* break, so P is not something you get to skip. The real choice is **C or A, during a partition**. A **bank balance** should pick **C** (better to say "try again" than let money be spent twice). A **like count** should pick **A** (better to show 1,203 likes when the truth is 1,207 than to show an error).

## The intuition

Imagine a small bank with **two branches**, one in Chennai and one in Madurai. Both keep a paper ledger for the same customer, Ravi, who has **₹10,000**. Every time money moves, the branches phone each other so both ledgers match.

One morning the **phone line is cut**. Ravi walks into Chennai and asks to withdraw ₹8,000. At the same time his brother, holding Ravi's joint-account card, walks into Madurai and asks to withdraw ₹8,000.

Each branch manager has two options:
1. **Say "Sorry, we can't confirm your balance right now. Please come back later."** The ledgers stay correct, but the customer is turned away. That is choosing **Consistency** over Availability.
2. **Pay out the ₹8,000 based on the local ledger.** The customer is happy, but now ₹16,000 has left a ₹10,000 account. That is choosing **Availability** over Consistency.

There is no third option that is both instant and correct, because Chennai simply **cannot know** what Madurai did while the line is down. That is the whole theorem.

Now replace the bank with a "like" button on a photo. If Chennai shows 1,203 likes and Madurai shows 1,207 for a few minutes, nobody loses money. Showing an error page would be worse. Same theorem, **different right answer**.

Terms:
- **Node**: one machine (server) in the system.
- **Replica**: a copy of the same data on another node.
- **Partition**: some nodes cannot talk to others, because of a cut cable, a bad switch, a cloud zone outage or even a long garbage-collection pause that looks like silence.
- **Stale read**: reading an old value that has already been changed somewhere else.
- **Eventual consistency**: if writes stop, all replicas will *eventually* agree, but in the meantime they may differ.

## How it actually works

### 1. What the three letters precisely mean

The formal version (proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, after Eric Brewer's 2000 talk) is narrower than most people think:

| Letter | Precise meaning | What it does NOT mean |
|---|---|---|
| C | **Linearizability**: all operations look like they happened in one single order on one copy | Not the "C" in ACID, which is about rules like "balance never negative" |
| A | **Every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response**, eventually | Not "99.99% uptime" or "fast" |
| P | System keeps working when **any number of messages are lost** between nodes | Not something you can switch off |

So the theorem is about **one specific strong kind of consistency** versus **one specific total kind of availability**, during **one specific failure**.

### 2. Why P is not optional

In any system with more than one machine talking over a network, partitions happen: a top-of-rack switch fails, a cloud availability zone loses connectivity, a node pauses for 20 seconds. You cannot "choose CA" and declare that the network will never fail. If you build as if it won't, then when it does, your system will break in an **unplanned** way, which is worse than either planned choice.

So "CA" really only makes sense for a **single machine** (a single Postgres server is consistent and available, until that one box dies). Once you replicate, you are designing for partitions.

### 3. The decision during a partition

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  W[Write or read arrives] --> N{Can reach other replicas}
  N -->|Yes| OK[Normal path]
  OK --> PL{Wait for replicas}
  PL -->|Yes| LC[Slower but consistent]
  PL -->|No| LL[Faster but maybe stale]
  N -->|No, partition| PC{Correct or answer now}
  PC -->|Correct| CP[CP: reject or wait]
  PC -->|Answer now| AP[AP: serve local data]
  AP --> RC[Reconcile later]
```

- **CP system**: on the side of the partition that cannot reach a **majority** (a **quorum**, more than half the replicas), it refuses writes, and often reads too. The majority side keeps working. Examples: systems built on consensus protocols like **Raft** or **Paxos** (etcd, ZooKeeper, Google Spanner, CockroachDB).
- **AP system**: every side keeps accepting reads and writes using local data. When the network heals, replicas **reconcile**: merge or pick a winner. Examples: **Cassandra** and **DynamoDB-style** stores in their default low-quorum modes, DNS, CDN caches.

Many databases are **tunable**. In Cassandra you can choose the consistency level per query: `ONE` leans AP, `QUORUM` on both reads and writes leans CP. So "Cassandra is AP" is a default, not a law.

### 4. Quorums in small numbers

Say you keep **N = 3** replicas. You write to **W** of them and read from **R** of them before replying.

- If **R + W > N** (for example W = 2, R = 2), every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read normally sees the latest write. But during a partition, a side with only 1 replica cannot gather 2, so it must **refuse**. That is the CP lean.
- If **W = 1, R = 1**, any single replica can answer. Always available, but reads can be stale. That is the AP lean.

### 5. Eventual consistency and conflict resolution

AP systems promise that replicas will converge. When two sides both accepted writes, something has to decide the final value:
- **Last-writer-wins (LWW)**: keep the write with the latest timestamp. Simple, but it silently **drops** one write, and clocks drift.
- **Merge by design**: use data types that can always be combined. A like counter can keep a per-replica count and add them up (a **CRDT**, conflict-free replicated data type). A shopping cart can union the items.
- **Ask the application or user**: keep both versions and resolve later.

This is why AP works beautifully for counters and carts, and badly for "only 1 unit left".

### 6. PACELC: the part that matters every day

Partitions are rare. Most of the time the network is fine. Daniel Abadi's **PACELC** extends CAP:

> **If P**artition, choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse (normal operation), choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency.

Even with no failure, keeping replicas in sync means **waiting**: for a quorum, maybe in another city. A cross-region round trip (Mumbai to Singapore) can add 50-70 ms to every write. So:
- **PC/EC** (Spanner-like): consistent always, pays latency always.
- **PA/EL** (Cassandra-like defaults): available in partitions, fast normally, stale reads possible.
- Mixed choices exist, and many systems let you pick **per operation**.

PACELC explains your p99 latency far more often than CAP explains an outage.

### 7. Choosing per operation, not per company

A single app usually needs both. A sketch in Java of how a service might route by need:

```java
enum Need { STRONG, FAST }

Balance readBalance(String accountId) {
    // money: must reflect every committed debit
    return ledgerStore.read(accountId, Need.STRONG); // leader or quorum read
}

long readLikes(String postId) {
    // social signal: a few seconds stale is fine
    return likeCache.getOrDefault(postId, 0L);       // nearest replica or cache
}
```

## A worked example

**A Flipkart-like marketplace during a big festive sale**, with data replicated across two data centres, DC-1 and DC-2. At 12:05 am the link between them drops for 90 seconds.

1. **Wallet and bank balance (CP).** A user in Chennai tries to pay ₹2,000 from a stored wallet. The wallet service uses a consensus-backed store with 3 replicas: 2 in DC-1, 1 in DC-2. Users routed to DC-1 still have a majority and pay normally. A user routed to DC-2 gets "Payment could not be confirmed, please retry" for those 90 seconds. Annoying, but **no wallet goes negative and no money is spent twice**. That is a deliberate CP choice.

2. **Inventory reservation for a limited deal (CP).** A phone deal has **50 units**. If both DCs kept selling independently, each might sell 50, giving 100 orders for 50 phones, and 50 angry cancellations next morning. So reservations go through the **single owner of that SKU's stock count** (the majority side). The minority side shows "Unable to add to cart, try again". A smart team narrows the blast radius: only the *reserve* step is CP; the product page itself still loads.

3. **Likes, view counts, "1,240 people bought this" (AP).** Both DCs keep counting locally. During the 90 seconds, DC-1 shows 1,240 and DC-2 shows 1,236. When the link heals, per-DC counters are summed and both show 1,251. **No user can tell, and nobody saw an error.**

4. **Product reviews (AP).** A review posted in DC-2 appears in DC-1 about 90 seconds later. Eventual consistency is fine here. One small fix improves experience: **read-your-own-writes**, meaning the person who posted the review sees it immediately because their session reads from the replica they wrote to.

5. **Normal times (PACELC).** With no partition, the wallet still pays a quorum write cost (around 10-20 ms within a region), while likes are written to the local replica in under 2 ms. The team **accepts latency for money and buys speed for social signals**.

The lesson for a design review: **list each piece of data, ask "what is the cost of a stale or conflicting value?", and pick C or A per piece**.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Pick any 2 of the 3."** You can't really drop P in a distributed system. The honest version is: **when a partition happens, pick C or A**. When there is no partition, you can have both.
- **"My database is CP (or AP), full stop."** Most modern stores are **tunable per query** (Cassandra levels, DynamoDB strongly consistent reads, MongoDB read and write concerns). The label describes defaults and configuration.
- **"The C in CAP is the C in ACID."** CAP's C is **linearizability**, about replicas agreeing. ACID's C is about the database enforcing rules such as constraints. Different ideas, same letter.
- **"Choosing A means the data is wrong."** It means data may be **stale for a while**, and conflicts must be **resolved by design**. For counters and carts, that can be perfectly correct in the end.
- **"CP means the system goes down."** Usually only the **minority side** of the partition refuses requests; the majority keeps working. Good design also limits CP to the few operations that truly need it.
- **"CAP is what makes my system slow."** Day to day, slowness comes from the **latency vs consistency** trade-off (PACELC), not from partitions.

## How to say it in an interview

*"CAP says that when data is replicated and the network splits, a node can either stay consistent by refusing or delaying requests it can't confirm, or stay available by answering from local data that might be stale. Partitions are a fact of life, so the real choice is consistency versus availability during a partition, and I make that choice per piece of data, not per system. For a wallet balance or a limited-stock reservation, a stale answer means real money lost or orders we can't fulfil, so I go CP: quorum or leader-based writes, and the minority side returns a retryable error. For likes, view counts and reviews, an error is worse than a slightly old number, so I go AP with eventual consistency and mergeable counters. I also think about PACELC: even without failures, strong consistency costs latency, so I only pay it where correctness demands it."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *Is "CA" ever valid?* Only for a single node or a system that never replicates over a network. The moment you replicate, partitions are possible and you must decide what happens then.
- *How do AP systems fix conflicts?* Last-writer-wins (simple, can lose data), mergeable data types like CRDT counters and sets, or keeping multiple versions for the app to resolve.
- *How would you make the CP path less painful for users?* Keep the CP part small (just the reserve or debit step), place a majority of replicas where most traffic is, return clear retryable errors, and use idempotency keys so retries don't double-charge.

## Key takeaways

- CAP is about **one moment: a network partition** between replicas.
- **C** = every read sees the latest write; **A** = every working node answers; **P** = survive lost messages.
- **P is not optional** once you replicate, so the real choice is **C vs A during a partition**.
- **Money and scarce stock lean CP**; **likes, views and reviews lean AP**.
- AP needs **eventual consistency** plus a **conflict-resolution plan** (LWW, CRDTs, merges).
- **PACELC**: with no partition, you still trade **latency vs consistency** every request.
- Decide **per operation**, and most databases let you tune it per query.

## Check yourself

1. A friend says "we chose CA, because our network is reliable." What is wrong with that?
   Answer: Any replicated system can see partitions, so you cannot opt out of P. Saying CA just means nobody decided what happens when the network splits, so the behaviour then will be accidental.
2. With N = 3 replicas, W = 2 and R = 2, what happens on a side of a partition that holds only one replica?
   Answer: It cannot reach 2 replicas, so it cannot complete quorum reads or writes and must refuse or wait. That is the CP behaviour, while the 2-replica side keeps working.
3. Why is AP fine for a like counter but risky for a "last 5 units" deal?
   Answer: Like counts from both sides can simply be added together later, so nothing is lost. Stock reservations on both sides can sell more units than exist, and that cannot be merged away; it becomes cancelled orders.
4. Your system has no outages, yet writes are slow because they wait for a replica in another region. Which idea explains this?
   Answer: PACELC: even with no partition, you trade latency for consistency. Waiting for remote replicas gives consistency at the cost of latency.

question: How can a streaming app show an IPL final live to crores of people at once without buffering, even on weak mobile networks?
answer:
## The short answer

No single server, and no single data centre, can send a live match to crores of phones at once. The bandwidth needed is simply too large. So live streaming apps split the problem into a few simple ideas:

1. **Encode** the camera feed into several copies at different qualities (for example 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p). These copies are called **renditions**.
2. **Chop** each copy into small **segments** of a few seconds each, and publish a **playlist** (a small text file) that lists them. The standard formats are **HLS** and **DASH**.
3. Let the **player on the phone choose** which quality to download for each segment, based on how fast the network is right now. This is **adaptive bitrate (ABR)** streaming. A weak 4G signal gets 360p instead of a frozen screen.
4. Serve the segments from a **CDN (content delivery network)**: thousands of **edge cache** servers spread across cities and inside telecom networks, close to viewers. An **origin shield** layer in the middle protects the source from being flooded.
5. Accept a few seconds of **delay behind the real match** in exchange for a buffer that hides network hiccups, and **pre-warm** capacity before the big moments (toss, last over, a Kohli six).

## The intuition

Think of a newspaper. The printing press (the **origin**) cannot drive to every home in India, so bundles go to regional depots, then to street vendors (**edge caches**). You buy from the corner vendor, not the press.

Now imagine a fresh **page every 4 seconds** (a **segment**), printed in three sizes: broadsheet, tabloid and pocket (**renditions**). The vendor gets each page once and hands copies to everyone. When your hands are full (weak network) you take the pocket edition; when free, the broadsheet. That page-by-page choice is **adaptive bitrate**.

Terms used below:
- **Bitrate**: how many bits per second a video needs. 3 Mbps means 3 megabits every second.
- **Encoder**: software that compresses raw video (for example H.264) at a target bitrate.
- **Rendition**: one quality version of the stream, such as 720p at 3 Mbps.
- **Segment**: a short chunk of video, typically 2 to 6 seconds, stored as a small file.
