- **Playlist / manifest**: a text file listing the segments. HLS calls it an `.m3u8` file, DASH calls it an `.mpd` file.
- **CDN**: a large network of cache servers that store copies of content near users.
- **Origin**: the source servers where segments are first created.
- **Latency (glass-to-glass)**: delay between something happening in the stadium and it appearing on your screen.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why one server cannot do it: the bandwidth math

Start small. One viewer watching at 2 Mbps (a decent 480p to 720p mobile stream) needs 2 Mbps.

- 1,000 viewers need 2 Gbps. One good server can handle that.
- 1 lakh viewers need 200 Gbps. That is already more than a typical server network card (25 to 100 Gbps).
- 3 crore (30 million) viewers need **60 Tbps** (60,000 Gbps).

That is about **600 servers** with 100 Gbps cards running flat out, before any headroom. And putting them all in one Mumbai data centre fails anyway: the building's internet links and the long paths to Guwahati or Coimbatore would clog, and distance adds **round-trip time** to every download. So the answer must be **many servers, spread out, close to viewers**.

### 2. Encoding into an ABR ladder

The stadium feed reaches a **live encoder** in the cloud. It produces several renditions at once. This list is called the **bitrate ladder**:

| Rendition | Resolution | Bitrate (approx.) | Who gets it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 240p | 0.3 Mbps | Very weak 3G or crowded 4G |
| Mobile | 360p | 0.7 Mbps | Typical weak mobile |
| SD | 480p | 1.2 Mbps | Average 4G |
| HD | 720p | 3 Mbps | Good 4G or Wi-Fi |
| Full HD | 1080p | 6 Mbps | Broadband, smart TVs |

Exact numbers depend on codec and content. The encoder is a single point of failure, so it runs **redundantly**: two independent pipelines in different cloud zones.

### 3. Segments and the playlist (HLS / DASH)

Each rendition is cut into small segments, say **4 seconds** each. Every segment is a plain file served over normal **HTTP**, the same protocol as web pages. That is the key trick: ordinary web caches and CDNs already know how to serve HTTP files to millions of people.

A **master playlist** lists the renditions; a **media playlist** for each rendition lists the latest segments. For a live stream the media playlist is a sliding window that the player re-downloads every few seconds:

```
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:4
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:9120
#EXTINF:4.0,
720p/seg_9120.ts
#EXTINF:4.0,
720p/seg_9121.ts
#EXTINF:4.0,
720p/seg_9122.ts
```

When seg_9123 is ready, the oldest entry drops off and the new one is added. **HLS** (from Apple) and **DASH** (an open standard) work the same way.

### 4. Adaptive bitrate: the player decides

The server does not decide quality. The **player on the phone** does, before fetching each segment. A simple version:

```
buffer = seconds of video already downloaded but not yet played
speed  = measured throughput of the last few segment downloads

if buffer < 6 s:        pick the highest rendition below 0.5 x speed   // play safe
else if buffer > 20 s:  pick the highest rendition below 0.9 x speed   // be bolder
else:                   pick the highest rendition below 0.7 x speed
never jump up more than one step at a time
```

Example on a Rapido ride across Bengaluru:
- On Wi-Fi at home, downloads run at 15 Mbps. The player picks 1080p (6 Mbps). Buffer is 20 seconds.
- The rider gets on the bike; 4G speed drops to 2 Mbps. The next 1080p segment takes 12 seconds to download a 4-second chunk. The buffer shrinks from 20 to 12 seconds, and the player measures the new speed.
- For the next segment it picks 480p (1.2 Mbps). Each 4-second segment now downloads in about 2.4 seconds, so the buffer stops shrinking and slowly refills.
- In a dead zone near a flyover, speed falls to 0.5 Mbps. The player drops to 240p. The picture is blurry, but **it keeps playing**.
- Back in good coverage, it climbs up one rung at a time.

The **buffer** absorbs the bumps; the spinning wheel only appears when it reaches zero. Real players (ExoPlayer, AVPlayer, hls.js) use smarter rules, but the idea is the same.

### 5. CDNs and edge caches

Viewers never talk to the origin. DNS routing sends each phone to a **nearby edge server**: in the same city, or even inside the mobile operator's own network.

The magic is **cache hit ratio** for live video. In one city, 10 lakh people are all asking for the same file, `720p/seg_9122.ts`, within a few seconds of each other. The edge fetches it **once** and serves it 10 lakh times. Two details make this work:
- **Request collapsing**: if 5,000 requests for a new segment arrive before the edge has it, the edge sends only **one** request upstream and makes the rest wait for that one answer.
- **Short cache times for playlists, long for segments**: the playlist changes every few seconds, so it is cached for about a second; a segment never changes once written, so it can be cached for its whole useful life.

Big events often use **multiple CDNs**, with a steering service moving users away from one that struggles.

### 6. Origin shield

With 2,000 edges each asking the origin for every new segment in 5 renditions, the origin gets 10,000 requests every 4 seconds, far more during retries. An **origin shield** is a middle layer of a few regional caches: edges ask the shield, only the shield asks the origin, which now sees a handful of requests per segment.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Stadium camera feed] --> B[Live encoders x2]
  B --> C[Packager HLS and DASH]
  C --> D[Origin storage]
  D --> E[Origin shield]
  E --> F[Edge cache Mumbai]
  E --> G[Edge cache Chennai]
  E --> H[Edge inside telco network]
  F --> I[Phones pick quality via ABR]
  G --> I
  H --> I
```

### 7. Live latency versus buffering

Here is the core trade-off. A player usually stays **about three segments behind** the newest one, so it always has something buffered. With 6-second segments that is roughly 18 seconds, plus encoding and CDN time: **20 to 30 seconds** behind the stadium. Your neighbour on TV or a WhatsApp group shouts "SIX!" before you see it.

- **Bigger buffer**: fewer stalls on weak networks, but more delay.
- **Smaller buffer and shorter segments**: closer to live, but any network wobble causes a stall, and the CDN gets more requests (more, smaller files).

**Low-latency HLS/DASH** send small **parts** of a segment while it is still being written, bringing delay to about **3 to 8 seconds**. For crores of viewers on patchy networks, many apps choose 10 to 20 seconds, because **not stalling matters more than being two seconds faster**. It is a product decision as much as an engineering one.

### 8. Traffic spikes and pre-warming

Concurrency jumps at the toss, each innings start, a tight last over, a star walking out to bat. The dangerous part is often **not video** but login, entitlement checks (is this user allowed to watch?), home page and ads.

Teams prepare by:
- **Pre-warming**: telling CDNs the expected peak in advance, and scaling origin, auth and APIs **before** the match, because autoscaling is too slow for a 2-minute surge.
- **Graceful degradation**: cap top quality at 720p during extreme peaks; turn off non-essential features; serve a cached home page.
- **Retry with jitter**, so phones do not all retry in the same second.

### 9. What the record numbers tell us

Indian cricket streaming has publicly reported some of the largest live audiences anywhere. For example, JioCinema **reported** a peak of around 3.2 crore concurrent viewers during the IPL 2023 final, and Disney+ Hotstar **reported** a peak of around 5.9 crore during the India vs New Zealand 2023 World Cup semi-final. Counting methods are not public, but the scale is clear: tens of terabits per second.

## A worked example

**A Hotstar-like app streaming the IPL final, 3 crore peak viewers.**

1. **Weeks before**: expected peak is 3.5 crore at 1.8 Mbps, about 63 Tbps. The team books capacity on three CDNs and load-tests login at 2x peak.
2. **Two hours before**: auth and ad services are scaled out manually; the home page is cached. Segments are 4 seconds, target delay about 15 seconds.
3. **Toss**: 80 lakh users open the app in five minutes; the pre-scaled login path holds.
4. **Play**: a user in Madurai on crowded 4G starts at 360p, measures 2.5 Mbps and steps up to 480p, then 720p. A Delhi user on fibre goes to 1080p.
5. **Edge behaviour**: the Chennai edge gets 6 lakh requests for each new 720p segment, but sends one request to the shield, which sends one to the origin.
6. **Last over, 15 off 6**: concurrency peaks at 3 crore and bandwidth nears the limit, so the control room caps quality at 720p for 10 minutes. Few notice on a phone.
7. **A problem**: one CDN's Kolkata region returns errors. Steering moves requests to another CDN; players retry while playing from their buffer, so nobody stalls.
8. **After the match**: the team reviews rebuffering ratio, average bitrate per city and peak Tbps for next season.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Just add more servers in our data centre."** The bottleneck is network paths and distance, not CPU; capacity must be spread across cities.
- **"The server decides the video quality."** In HLS and DASH the **player** decides, segment by segment, using its own measured speed and buffer level. The server just offers the choices.
- **"Live video is too fresh to cache."** Each segment is fetched by lakhs within seconds, so it caches extremely well.
- **"Lower latency is always better."** It means a smaller buffer and more stalls on weak networks.
- **"Autoscaling will handle the spike."** New servers take minutes; the spike takes seconds. **Pre-scale**.
- **"Video traffic is the hardest part."** Failures often hit login, entitlement or home-page APIs, which are not cached like segments.

## How to say it in an interview

*"One server can't do it because of bandwidth: 3 crore viewers at 2 Mbps is about 60 terabits per second, far beyond any single site. So first, the live feed is encoded into a ladder of qualities, say 240p to 1080p. Each quality is chopped into segments of a few seconds and listed in a playlist, using HLS or DASH over plain HTTP. The player on the phone uses adaptive bitrate: before each segment it looks at its measured speed and buffer, and picks the best quality it can sustain, so a weak network gets 360p instead of a spinning wheel. Segments are served by CDNs from edge caches close to users, often inside telecom networks. Everyone wants the same segment at once, so the edge fetches it once and serves it lakhs of times, and an origin shield protects the origin. A bigger buffer means fewer stalls but more lag. For big matches we pre-warm CDN and backend capacity, use multiple CDNs, and can cap top quality at peak."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *Why use HTTP segments instead of a continuous stream like RTMP or WebRTC?* HTTP files can be cached by ordinary CDNs and scale to crores of viewers; WebRTC gives sub-second delay but each viewer needs a live connection, which is much harder and costlier to scale.
- *How would you measure stream quality?* Rebuffering ratio, start time, average bitrate and failure rate, by city, operator and device.
- *What if the origin goes down?* A redundant encoder and origin in another zone take over, and the player switches to the backup playlist URL.

## Key takeaways

- **Bandwidth math** rules it out for one server: crores of viewers times a few Mbps is tens of Tbps.
- Encode into a **bitrate ladder** of several qualities.
- **HLS/DASH** cut video into small HTTP **segments** listed in a **playlist**.
- **Adaptive bitrate** lets the player pick quality per segment from its speed and buffer, trading sharpness for smooth playback.
- **CDN edge caches** near users serve the same segment to lakhs; **request collapsing** and an **origin shield** protect the source.
- **Latency vs buffering** is a real trade-off; low-latency HLS/DASH reduce delay at the cost of stall risk.
- **Pre-warm and pre-scale** for predictable spikes; protect login and APIs, not just video.

## Check yourself

1. Roughly how much bandwidth do 1 crore viewers at an average of 1.5 Mbps need, and why does this rule out a single data centre?
   Answer: 1 crore x 1.5 Mbps = 15 Tbps. That is far beyond one site's network links, and long paths to distant viewers would be slow, so delivery must be spread over many edge caches close to users.
2. A user's speed drops from 8 Mbps to 1 Mbps mid-match. What does an ABR player do, and why does the screen not freeze?
   Answer: It notices slow downloads and a shrinking buffer, and picks a lower rendition such as 360p or 480p for the next segments. The existing buffer keeps the video playing while it switches, so quality drops instead of the video stalling.
3. Why can live segments be cached for a long time but the live playlist only for about a second?
   Answer: A segment file never changes once written, so it is safe to cache. The playlist changes every few seconds as new segments are added, so long caching would make players miss new segments.
4. Your product head wants the stream to be only 3 seconds behind live for all users. What is the trade-off you would explain?
   Answer: Low-latency HLS or DASH can get close, but a tiny buffer means more stalls on weak mobile networks and more small requests. Offer it on good networks, keep a larger buffer on weak ones.

question: How does a "Your order is out for delivery" notification reach your phone even when the app is closed?
answer:
## The short answer

Your shopping app is **not** the thing that receives the message. When the app is closed it isn't running at all, so it can't listen for anything. Instead, the **phone's operating system** keeps **one shared, always-on connection** to a push service run by the platform owner: **APNs** (Apple Push Notification service) on iPhones, and **FCM** (Firebase Cloud Messaging) on most Android phones.

The flow is:

1. When you install and open the app, it asks the OS for a **device token**: a long string that means "this app on this phone". The app sends that token to the company's server, which stores it against your user ID.
2. When your order goes out for delivery, the company's server sends a small message (a **payload**, at most about **4 KB**) plus your token to APNs or FCM.
3. APNs or FCM pushes it down the phone's existing connection. The **OS** shows the banner, even though the app never woke up.

Push delivery is **best-effort**: messages can be late, merged or dropped. So the app must always **fetch the true order status from the server when it opens**, and never treat the notification as the source of truth.

## The intuition

Think of a big apartment building with a **security guard at the gate**. Couriers don't wander to every flat and wait outside each door; that would be chaos. Every courier hands parcels to the one guard, and the guard has the flat number for each resident. When a parcel arrives, the guard rings the intercom of the right flat.

- The **building** is your phone.
- The **flats** are the apps on it. They can be fast asleep (closed).
- The **guard** is the OS plus APNs or FCM. One guard, one gate, for all apps.
- The **flat number** is the **device token**.
- The **courier** is the company's backend, for example a Flipkart-like order system.

If each app kept its own line open, that is 40 couriers camping outside 40 doors all day, and the battery drains fast.

Terms used below:
- **Push notification**: a message the server sends to the phone without the phone asking for it first.
- **Payload**: the message content, usually JSON.
- **Device token** (also called registration token in FCM): an opaque ID issued by APNs or FCM that addresses one app install on one device.
- **Best-effort**: the system tries hard, but promises nothing about delivery or timing.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why apps can't just keep their own connection open

A phone saves battery mainly by letting its **radio** (the Wi-Fi or mobile data chip) sleep. Any open network connection needs small "I'm still here" packets, called **keep-alives** or heartbeats, every few minutes, or routers and mobile networks silently drop it. Each heartbeat wakes the radio, and the radio stays in a high-power state for several seconds afterwards.

Thirty apps each doing this on their own schedule means the radio almost never sleeps. So both iOS and Android **stop or freeze background apps**: iOS suspends them within seconds of leaving the screen, and Android's **Doze mode** and **app standby** restrict network access for idle apps. The OS keeps **one** connection, shared by all apps, with a carefully tuned heartbeat. That single connection is the only door in.

### 2. Registration: getting the device token

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[App opens first time] --> B[Ask user for permission]
  B --> C[OS registers with APNs or FCM]
  C --> D[Device token returned]
  D --> E[App sends token to backend]
  E --> F[Token stored with user ID]
```

- On iOS the user must **grant permission** to show alerts. On Android 13 and later, the app must also ask for a notification permission.
- The token is tied to **app plus device**, not to the person. One user with a phone and a tablet has two tokens. Reinstalling the app usually gives a new token.
- The backend stores rows like `user_id, token, platform, last_seen`.

### 3. Sending: the four hops

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  O[Order service] --> K[Event queue]
  K --> N[Notification service]
  N --> P[Prefs and quiet hours]
  P --> AP[APNs]
  P --> FC[FCM]
  AP --> PH[Phone OS]
  FC --> PH
  PH --> U[Banner on screen]
```

1. The **order service** marks the order `OUT_FOR_DELIVERY` and publishes an event to a queue such as Kafka.
2. A separate **notification service** consumes the event. It looks up the user's tokens, checks **preferences** (did they turn off order updates?) and **quiet hours**, picks the language, and builds the payload.
3. It calls APNs (an HTTP/2 API, authenticated with a signed token from Apple) or FCM (an HTTPS API, authenticated with a Google service account), once per device token.
4. APNs or FCM finds the device's live connection and pushes the message. If the phone is offline, the service holds it for a while and tries when the phone reconnects.
5. On the phone, the **OS** shows the banner itself. The app only runs when the user taps it, or if the message is a special background type.

Keeping the notification service separate means the order service never slows down because Apple is slow.

### 4. The payload, priority and collapse keys

A typical alert payload:

```
APNs body (headers: apns-push-type=alert, apns-priority=10, apns-collapse-id=order-OD4471)
{ "aps": { "alert": { "title": "Out for delivery", "body": "Your order will arrive today by 7 PM" },
           "sound": "default" },
  "order_id": "OD4471", "deeplink": "app://orders/OD4471" }

FCM v1 request
{ "message": { "token": "<device token>",
    "notification": { "title": "Out for delivery", "body": "Arriving today by 7 PM" },
    "data": { "order_id": "OD4471" },
    "android": { "priority": "high", "collapse_key": "order-OD4471", "ttl": "3600s" } } }
```

| Knob | What it does | Typical setting |
|---|---|---|
| **Payload size** | Max about **4 KB** on both. Send IDs and short text, not the whole order. | Order ID plus a deep link |
| **Priority** | High: deliver now, may wake the device. Normal: OS may delay to save battery. | High for delivery updates, normal for offers |
| **Collapse key** | If several messages with the same key are waiting, only the **latest** is shown. | One key per order |
| **TTL / expiration** | How long APNs or FCM keeps trying if the phone is offline. | Hours for delivery, zero for "your OTP" style messages that go stale |

Two details worth knowing. Platforms **watch how you use high priority**: if most high-priority messages produce nothing visible, Android may quietly downgrade them. And **silent or background pushes** (data only, to wake the app and refresh content) are throttled heavily on iOS, so don't build features that rely on them arriving.

### 5. Tokens go stale, so clean them up

Tokens stop working when the user uninstalls the app, reinstalls it, restores a new phone, or simply doesn't use it for a long time (Firebase documents that tokens inactive for about 270 days are treated as expired). Sending to dead tokens wastes quota and slows every campaign.

- APNs replies **410 Unregistered** (or 400 BadDeviceToken); FCM replies **UNREGISTERED** (HTTP 404). On these, **delete the token**.
- The app should **re-send its token on every app open**, because the OS can rotate it. Update `last_seen` each time.
- Periodically remove tokens not refreshed for a couple of months.

### 6. Sending to crores of users

One delivery update is easy. "Big sale starts at midnight" to **10 crore** (100 million) devices is a different problem.

- **Queue first.** The campaign tool writes jobs to a queue; a pool of sender workers drains it. If APNs slows down, the queue grows instead of the system falling over.
- **Batch and reuse connections.** Keep long-lived HTTP/2 connections to APNs, which allow many requests in flight on one connection. Send in parallel batches, and look up preferences and tokens in bulk.
- **Respect rate limits.** FCM has per-project quotas (sending above them returns 429 or "quota exceeded"); APNs can push back on overloaded connections. Use a **token bucket** limiter per provider, and **exponential backoff with jitter** on 429 and 5xx errors.
- **Separate lanes.** Transactional messages (OTP, out for delivery) get their own queue and workers so a 10-crore marketing blast never delays someone's OTP.
- **Spread it out.** Stagger campaigns over 15-30 minutes so the app's own servers survive the wave of people tapping at once.

```
// sender worker, simplified
while (true) {
  batch = queue.poll(500);
  for (msg : batch) {
    limiter.acquire(msg.provider);              // token bucket per APNs / FCM
    result = provider.send(msg.token, msg.payload);
    if (result.isUnregistered()) tokens.delete(msg.token);
    else if (result.isRetryable()) queue.retryLater(msg, backoffWithJitter(msg.attempt));
  }
}
```

### 7. Best-effort: design for the missing message

Neither Apple nor Google guarantees delivery. Messages can be:
- **dropped** (phone was offline past the TTL; APNs keeps only the **last** pending notification per app when a device is offline),
- **delayed** (battery saver, Doze, aggressive vendor battery managers on some Android phones),
- **collapsed** (only the newest of several with the same key),
- **hidden** (user turned notifications off at the OS level, which the server cannot see).

So the rule: **the push is a hint, the server is the truth.** When the app opens, it calls the order API and shows the real status. Anything important, such as a refund or an OTP, also needs another channel (SMS, email, in-app inbox) or a way to fetch it.

### 8. Preferences and quiet hours

Users who get annoyed **turn notifications off for good**, and that switch lives in the OS, beyond your reach. So the notification service should:
- keep per-user, per-category settings (order updates, offers, price drops);
- apply **quiet hours** (for example, no marketing between 10 PM and 8 AM in the user's time zone), while still allowing urgent transactional ones;
- cap frequency (for example, no more than three promotional pushes a day);

## A worked example

Priya orders headphones on a Flipkart-like app. Order ID OD4471.

1. **Monday, install.** She opens the app, taps Allow on the permission prompt. iOS registers with APNs and hands the app a token. The app sends it to `/devices/register`. The backend stores `priya, token_A, ios, last_seen=Mon`.
2. **Thursday, 9:40 AM.** The delivery partner scans the parcel onto a van. The logistics system marks OD4471 `OUT_FOR_DELIVERY` and publishes an event to Kafka.
3. **9:40:01.** The notification service consumes it. Priya has order updates on; quiet hours don't apply to transactional messages. It builds a 300-byte payload with `apns-collapse-id = order-OD4471`, high priority, a 6-hour expiry, and sends it to APNs over an already-open HTTP/2 connection. APNs replies 200.
4. **9:40:02.** Priya's phone, app closed, shows "Out for delivery. Arriving today by 7 PM". The app itself did not run.
5. **Noon.** Priya is in a basement with no signal. The van is delayed, so two more updates are sent: "Now arriving by 9 PM" and "Delivery attempt in 30 minutes". Because both use the same collapse ID, when she comes back online she sees only the latest. Good: the old ETA would only confuse her.
6. **She taps the banner.** The app opens at the deep link, calls the order API and shows the live map and status. Even if every push had been lost, this screen would still be correct.
7. **Old tablet.** Priya also had `token_B` from a tablet she reset months ago. APNs returned 410 Unregistered for it, and the service deleted that row.
8. **That night**, a sale campaign runs through the separate marketing queue; Priya's quiet hours start at 10 PM, so hers is skipped.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The app is running quietly in the background, listening."** It usually isn't. The OS and APNs or FCM do the listening; the app is often fully suspended or killed.
- **"If the API returned 200, the user saw it."** A 200 only means APNs or FCM **accepted** it. The phone may be off, the user may have muted the app, or the message may expire.
- **"A device token identifies the user."** It identifies one app install on one device. Users have several, and tokens change.
- **"Push is a good way to send data to the app."** Payloads are about 4 KB and may be lost. Send a short message and an ID; the app fetches the real data.
- **"High priority for everything makes it faster."** Platforms deprioritise apps that abuse it. Keep it for time-sensitive messages.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Apps can't keep their own connection open when closed, because the OS suspends them to save battery: every open connection needs heartbeats that wake the radio. Instead the OS keeps one shared connection to the platform push service, APNs on iOS and FCM on Android. When the app first runs, it gets a device token from the OS and registers it with our backend against the user. When the order goes out for delivery, the order service publishes an event; a separate notification service checks the user's preferences and quiet hours, builds a small payload under 4 KB with a priority, collapse key and expiry, and sends it to APNs or FCM with the token. They push it over the phone's connection and the OS shows the banner. I'd remove tokens when APNs or FCM say they're unregistered, put big campaigns on a separate queue with rate limiting and backoff, and remember delivery is best-effort, so the app always fetches the real order status when it opens."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *How do you know if the user actually saw it?* You don't, from the send response. Track opens by having the app report when a notification is tapped, and for critical messages add a fallback channel such as SMS.
- *How would you send a sale alert to 10 crore users?* Precompute the audience, enqueue jobs, use many sender workers with per-provider rate limits and connection reuse, skip dead tokens and opted-out users, and stagger over 15-30 minutes so the app backend can absorb the opens.

## Key takeaways

- A closed app can't listen; the **OS holds one shared connection** to **APNs or FCM** to save battery.
- The **device token** addresses one app on one device; the backend stores it per user and refreshes it on every open.
- Flow: **order service, queue, notification service, APNs or FCM, phone OS**.
- Keep payloads **small (about 4 KB max)**; use **priority**, **collapse keys** and **expiry** deliberately.
- **Delete tokens** that come back unregistered, and prune stale ones.
- At crore scale, use **queues, batching, rate limits, backoff, separate lanes and staggering**.
- Delivery is **best-effort**: the push is a hint, the **server is the source of truth**.
- Respect **preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps**, or users switch you off permanently.

## Check yourself

1. Why doesn't every app simply keep its own socket open to its own server, like a chat app on a laptop?
   Answer: Each connection needs regular heartbeats that wake the phone's radio, and many apps doing this would drain the battery. So the OS suspends background apps and keeps one shared connection to APNs or FCM instead.
2. APNs returns 410 Unregistered for one of a user's tokens. What should the backend do and why?
   Answer: Delete that token, because the app was uninstalled or the token was replaced. Continuing to send wastes quota and slows large campaigns, and the user's other valid tokens still work.
3. Three delivery updates for the same order are sent while the phone is offline. What does the user see when it reconnects, if you used a collapse key per order?
   Answer: Only the latest update, because messages with the same collapse key replace older pending ones. That is what you want for a changing status like an ETA.
4. A user says they never got the out-for-delivery push, but the API call returned success. How should the app be designed so this doesn't hurt them?
   Answer: Success only means the push service accepted it; delivery is best-effort. The app should fetch the real order status from the server whenever it opens, and critical messages should have a fallback such as SMS or an in-app inbox.

question: When you open Instagram, how is your feed built so fast? What are fan-out on write and fan-out on read, and what happens when a celebrity with crores of followers posts?
answer:
## The short answer

When you open an Instagram-like app, the feed is fast because **most of the work was done before you opened it**. Each user has a ready-made **feed list** (a short list of post IDs) sitting in an in-memory cache such as **Redis**. Opening the app just reads the top 20 IDs from that list, fetches those posts, ranks them and shows them.

There are two ways to fill that list:

- **Fan-out on write (push):** when someone posts, the system copies the post ID into the feed list of **every follower**, right away. Reads become cheap; writes become expensive.
- **Fan-out on read (pull):** nothing is copied at post time. When you open the app, the system **goes and collects** recent posts from everyone you follow and merges them. Writes are cheap; reads are expensive.

The **celebrity problem**: if an account with 10 crore followers posts, fan-out on write means 10 crore list inserts for one photo. So real systems use a **hybrid**: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities, and merge the two when you open the app.

## The intuition

Think of getting your news in the morning.

- **Newspaper delivery (fan-out on write):** the paper is printed once, and the delivery boy drops a copy at every subscriber's door before 6 am. When you wake up, the paper is already there. Reading is instant. But the delivery work happens for every subscriber, even the ones who never read it.
- **Going to the shop (fan-out on read):** nobody delivers anything. When you want news, you walk to the shop and pick up the papers you like. No wasted delivery, but you wait every time you want to read.

Now imagine a paper with 10 crore subscribers. Door-to-door delivery for every copy would take forever. So for that one huge paper, you keep a big stack at the shop counter and people pick it up when they come. Your small local papers are still delivered. That mix is the **hybrid approach**.

Terms used below:

- **Follower:** someone who follows an account and should see its posts.
- **Feed:** the list of posts you see when you open the app.
- **Fan-out:** copying one thing (a post) out to many places (followers' feeds).
- **Cache:** fast memory storage (like Redis) that keeps hot data close, so we avoid slow database reads.
- **Post ID:** a small unique number for a post. Feeds store IDs, not the full photo or caption.
- **Hydration:** turning a list of IDs into full posts (caption, image URL, like count) by looking them up.
- **Cursor:** a bookmark that says "give me posts older than this one", used for scrolling.
- **Crore:** 1 crore = 10 million. **Lakh:** 1 lakh = 100,000.

## How it actually works

### 1. The data we keep

An Instagram-like system has, roughly:

- A **post store**: post ID, author, caption, media URL, created time. Usually a database plus a post cache.
- A **follow graph**: who follows whom. "Give me all followers of user X" must be fast.
- A **feed cache per user**: a list of the most recent few hundred post IDs for that user's home feed.

Storing only IDs keeps feed lists tiny. If each entry is a post ID plus a timestamp (about 16 bytes), 500 entries is about 8 KB per user. For 10 crore daily active users that is about 800 GB of memory, which a Redis cluster can hold. Users who have not opened the app in weeks usually do not get a cached feed at all.

### 2. Fan-out on write (push)

When user A posts:

1. Save the post in the post store.
2. Put a "fan out post P" job on a queue (like Kafka), so the user does not wait.
3. Workers read A's follower list in batches and, for each follower F, add P to F's feed list.
4. Trim each list so it never grows past, say, 500 entries.

In Redis, with a sorted set (a set where each item has a score, here the timestamp):

```
ZADD   feed:{followerId}  1760500000123  post:98765    # score = post time in ms
ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:{followerId} 0 -501              # keep only newest 500
```

**Cost math, small numbers first.** You have 300 followers. One post means 300 inserts. Easy.

Now scale up. Say 5 crore posts a day, and the average poster has 200 followers. That is 5 crore x 200 = **1,000 crore (10 billion) feed inserts a day**, about **1.2 lakh inserts per second** on average, and several times that at peak. Large, but spread across many machines it is manageable, because each insert is a tiny in-memory write.

The payoff: **reads are cheap**. Opening the app is one call: "give me the top 20 of my list". That is usually a few milliseconds.

### 3. Fan-out on read (pull)

When you open the app:

1. Look up everyone you follow, say 400 accounts.
2. For each, fetch their recent posts (from each author's own "my posts" list).
3. Merge all of them by time (or score), take the top 20.

Posting is now one write. But every app open does about 400 lookups and a merge. If reads happen 50-100 times more often than posts (people scroll far more than they post), you are doing the expensive work on the busy side. It also makes latency worse: your feed is only as fast as the slowest of those 400 lookups.

Fan-out on read does have real strengths: no wasted work for inactive users, new follows show up instantly, and there is no huge write storm.

### 4. The celebrity problem

A film star with **10 crore followers** posts one photo. With pure push:

- 10 crore inserts for one post.
- Even at a dedicated 10 lakh inserts per second, that is **100 seconds** of work, and it delays everyone else's fan-out jobs in the same queue.
- Most of those followers will not open the app in the next hour, so much of that work is wasted.
- If the star posts five times during a cricket match, that is 50 crore inserts.

This is sometimes called the **hot key** or **write amplification** problem: one action turns into a huge number of writes.

### 5. The hybrid approach

Pick a threshold, for example **1 lakh followers** (the exact number depends on your system and is tuned with data).

- **Normal accounts (below threshold):** fan-out on write. Their posts are pushed into followers' feed lists.
- **Celebrity accounts (above threshold):** no fan-out. Their posts stay in their own "recent posts" list, which is extremely hot and cached in many replicas.
- **At read time:** fetch your precomputed feed list, then fetch recent posts from the few celebrities you follow (usually a small number, say 10-30), merge, rank, return.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[User posts] --> B{Celebrity author}
  B -- No --> C[Fan-out workers]
  C --> D[Follower feed lists]
  B -- Yes --> E[Celebrity post list]
  F[User opens app] --> G[Read own feed list]
  G --> H[Merge celebrity posts]
  E --> H
  D --> G
  H --> I[Rank and hydrate]
  I --> J[Show top 20]
```

Another common tweak:

- **Skip inactive followers.** During fan-out, only push to users active in the last few weeks. If an inactive user comes back, rebuild their feed with a one-time pull.

### 6. Pagination with cursors

You scroll, and the app asks for the next 20 posts. Using **page numbers or offsets** ("skip 20, take 20") breaks on a live feed: if 3 new posts arrived while you were reading, everything shifts down by 3 and you see duplicates.

So feeds use a **cursor**: the server returns the score (timestamp) of the last post it sent, and the next request says "give me 20 posts older than this".

```
first page:  ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 +inf -inf LIMIT 0 20
next page:   ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 (1760500000123 -inf LIMIT 0 20
             # "(" means strictly less than the cursor
```

The cursor is usually encoded into an opaque string so clients cannot depend on its format. Ties are broken by post ID. "Pull to refresh" does the reverse: "give me posts newer than the top one I have".

### 7. Ranking, briefly

Modern feeds are not purely by time. A simple pipeline:

1. **Candidate generation:** collect a few hundred candidates (your feed list, celebrity posts, maybe suggested posts).
2. **Scoring:** a model predicts how likely you are to like, comment, share or spend time on each post, using signals like how close you are to the author, post freshness and post type.
3. **Final touches:** remove duplicates, avoid five posts in a row from one author, mix in variety.

Fan-out solves "what could I see"; ranking decides "what order". Ranking is heavier, so it often runs on a smaller candidate set, and results for the first page may be precomputed when the user is likely to open the app.

### 8. Deletes, edits and unfollows

Because feed lists store **only IDs** and posts are **hydrated at read time**:

- **Edit:** nothing to update in feeds. The next hydration reads the new caption.
- **Delete:** mark the post as deleted in the post store. Hydration skips it. A background job may also remove the ID from feed lists, but correctness does not depend on it.
- **Unfollow or block:** filter at read time (check that you still follow the author), and clean up lazily.
- **Privacy change:** same idea, always re-check permissions at hydration. Never trust that an ID in a feed list is still allowed.

This is the key design choice: **the feed list is a hint, the post store is the truth**.

## A worked example

**A Hotstar-like or Instagram-like app during an India vs Pakistan match.**

1. Riya (300 followers) posts a photo of her living room watching the match. The post is saved, a fan-out job goes to Kafka, and within about a second, her 300 followers' Redis feed lists get her post ID. Her request returned in 80 ms; she never waited for the fan-out.
2. A famous cricketer with **8 crore followers** posts a celebration photo. His account is above the 1 lakh threshold, so there is **no fan-out**. The post goes into his own recent-posts list, which is replicated across many cache nodes because millions will read it.
3. Arjun opens the app. The feed service:
   - reads Arjun's feed list: top 200 IDs (including Riya's post);
   - sees that Arjun follows 12 celebrity accounts and fetches each one's latest posts (12 small reads, all cache hits);
   - merges about 260 candidates and sends them to ranking;
   - takes the top 20, hydrates them from the post cache (one batch lookup), filters out one post its author deleted 5 minutes ago, and returns.
   Total: about 100-150 ms.
4. Arjun scrolls. The app sends the cursor from the last post. The next 20 come from older entries, with no duplicates even though 15 new posts arrived meanwhile.
5. Riya edits her caption to add "What a six!". No feed list changes. Everyone who loads it now sees the new caption.
6. A follower of Riya who has not opened the app in 2 months was skipped during fan-out. When he returns, the system notices no cached feed, does a one-time **pull** from the accounts he follows, and stores the result as his new feed list.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The feed is built from scratch when you open the app."** For most systems, the expensive part is precomputed. Opening the app is mostly reading a cached list, merging a few extra sources, ranking and hydrating.
- **"Fan-out on write is always better because reads are fast."** It wastes work on inactive users and collapses under celebrity accounts. The right choice depends on the follower distribution and read/write ratio.
- **"Feed lists store the full posts."** They store IDs (and maybe a score). Full content is fetched at read time, which keeps memory small and makes edits and deletes simple.
- **"Deleting a post means removing it from crores of feed lists right away."** You mark it deleted and filter at read time. Cleanup in the lists can happen slowly in the background.
- **"Offset pagination is fine."** On a feed that changes every second, offsets cause duplicates and gaps. Use cursors.

## How to say it in an interview

*"An Instagram-like feed is fast because it is mostly precomputed. Each user has a feed list of recent post IDs in a cache like Redis. There are two ways to fill it. Fan-out on write pushes each new post ID into every follower's list at post time, so reads are a single cheap lookup but writes multiply by follower count. Fan-out on read does nothing at post time and gathers posts from everyone you follow when you open the app, which is cheap to write but slow and expensive to read. Since reads far outnumber writes, push is the default, but it breaks for celebrities: one post from a 10-crore-follower account means 10 crore inserts. So I'd use a hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for accounts above a follower threshold, and merge both at read time. Feed lists hold only IDs, posts are hydrated and permission-checked at read time so edits and deletes just work, I page with cursors instead of offsets, and a ranking model orders the candidates."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *How do you avoid wasting fan-out on inactive users?* Only push to users active recently; for a returning user, rebuild the feed once by pulling.
- *What if the fan-out workers fall behind?* The post is still saved; feeds are just slightly late. Monitor queue lag, add workers, and prioritise active followers. This is eventual consistency and is usually acceptable for feeds.
- *Why a sorted set instead of a list?* Scores (timestamps) make cursor paging easy and keep order correct even when inserts arrive out of order.

## Key takeaways

- Feeds are fast because they are **precomputed lists of post IDs** in a cache.
- **Fan-out on write** = cheap reads, expensive writes; **fan-out on read** = cheap writes, expensive reads.
- Reads far outnumber writes, so **push is the default** for normal accounts.
- **Celebrities break push**; use a **hybrid** with a follower threshold and merge at read time.
- Skip **inactive followers** during fan-out and rebuild their feeds on return.
- Use **cursor pagination**, not offsets, on live feeds.
- Store **IDs only** and **hydrate at read time**, so edits, deletes and privacy changes are handled by filtering.
- **Ranking** sits on top: candidates first, then a scoring model.

## Check yourself

1. A user with 500 followers posts once. How many feed inserts happen with fan-out on write, and how many with fan-out on read?
   Answer: About 500 inserts with fan-out on write (one per follower, fewer if inactive followers are skipped). Zero with fan-out on read; the work happens later when each follower opens the app.
2. Why is pure fan-out on write a bad idea for an account with 10 crore followers?
   Answer: One post becomes 10 crore writes, which takes a long time, delays other fan-out jobs, and is largely wasted on followers who will not open the app soon. A hybrid pulls that account's posts at read time instead.
3. A user scrolls to page 2 while 5 new posts arrive. Why does offset pagination show duplicates, and what fixes it?
   Answer: The new posts push everything down by 5, so "skip 20" now lands 5 positions earlier and repeats posts. A cursor (posts older than the last seen timestamp) always continues exactly where the user stopped.
4. A post is deleted after it was fanned out to 2 lakh feeds. How do you make sure nobody sees it?
   Answer: Mark it deleted in the post store and check that at hydration time, skipping deleted posts. Removing the ID from the 2 lakh feed lists can then happen lazily in the background.

question: Why can automatic retries turn a small slowdown into a full outage, and how do exponential backoff and jitter prevent it?
answer:
## The short answer

A **retry** means "the call failed, so try it again". One retry by one user is harmless. The danger is that **every caller retries at the same moment, for the same reason**. When a service slows down, its callers time out and send the request again, so the slow service now gets **two or three times its normal traffic** exactly when it is weakest. That extra load makes it slower, which causes more timeouts, which causes more retries. A small slowdown becomes a **retry storm** and then a full outage.

It gets worse with layers. If three layers of services each make 3 attempts, one user click can become **3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls** at the bottom.

The fixes:

- **Exponential backoff**: wait longer after each failure (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms...), so retries thin out instead of piling up.
- **Jitter**: add randomness to that wait, so thousands of clients do not all retry at the same instant.
- **Retry budgets**: cap retries at a small share of traffic (say 10%), so retries can never multiply load.
- Retry only **safe (idempotent) operations**, retry at **one layer only**, use **timeouts**, and add a **circuit breaker** to stop calling a service that is clearly down.

## The intuition

Picture a crowded mall entrance on the first day of a big sale. The automatic door jams and opens slowly. A few people push it. It does not open faster, so more people push, harder, all together. Now the door is jammed even worse, the motor trips, and nobody gets in. The door had a small problem. **The crowd's reaction turned it into a big one.**

Now give the crowd two rules: "if the door does not open, step back and wait longer each time" (**exponential backoff**), and "each person waits a slightly different, random time" (**jitter**). The door gets a few gentle, spread-out pushes, recovers, and people flow in.

Terms:

- **Retry**: automatically sending a failed request again.
- **Timeout**: how long a caller waits for a reply before giving up. A timeout does not cancel the work on the server; the server may still be processing it.
- **Transient failure**: a temporary failure that may succeed if tried again (a network blip, a busy server returning 503).
- **Retry storm**: a surge of traffic made mostly of retries, which overloads the service it is trying to reach.
- **Amplification**: how many real calls one original request turns into.
- **Thundering herd**: many clients waking up and hitting a service at exactly the same moment.
- **Idempotent**: doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. Reading a price is idempotent; "charge Rs 500" is not, unless it carries an idempotency key.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why a slowdown feeds itself

Start small. A pricing service normally gets **10,000 requests per second (RPS)** and can handle about **12,000 RPS**. It is comfortable, with 20% spare room.

Now its database gets slow for a minute. Replies that took 50 ms now take 2 seconds. Callers have a 1-second timeout, so many calls time out. Each caller retries up to 2 more times (3 attempts in total).

- If half the calls time out, load becomes 10,000 + 5,000 retries + some second retries, roughly **17,500 RPS**. That is above capacity.
- Above capacity, queues grow, replies get even slower, and now nearly all calls time out. Load heads towards **10,000 x 3 = 30,000 RPS**, **2.5 times what the service can handle**.
- Worse, the server is still working on requests whose callers already gave up.

Even when the database recovers, retry traffic alone keeps it overloaded: a **metastable failure**: the system stays broken after the original cause is gone, because the load itself keeps it broken.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Dependency slows down] --> B[Callers hit timeouts]
  B --> C[Callers retry]
  C --> D[Load rises 2x to 3x]
  D --> E[Queues grow, even slower]
  E --> B
  E --> F[Full outage]
  C -. backoff, jitter, budget .-> G[Retries spread and capped]
  G --> H[Service recovers]
```

### 2. Multiplication across layers

Real systems have layers. Say the app calls an API gateway, which calls the order service, which calls the inventory service. If **each layer** makes 3 attempts:

| Layer | Attempts per call | Calls reaching the next layer |
|---|---|---|
| App to gateway | 3 | 3 |
| Gateway to order service | 3 | 9 |
| Order service to inventory | 3 | **27** |

One user tap becomes **27 calls** to inventory in the worst case. If each layer does 1 try plus 3 retries (4 attempts), it is 4 x 4 x 4 = **64**. This is why the rule is: **retry at one layer only**, usually the one closest to the failure, and make the other layers fail fast.

### 3. The thundering herd after recovery

Suppose a login service is down for 30 seconds. Two lakh (200,000) app users are waiting. If every app retries "every 5 seconds", they all fall into the same rhythm. When the service comes back, it gets **200,000 requests in the same second**, falls over again, and the cycle repeats.

The cause is **synchronisation**: clients that failed together keep retrying together. Backoff alone does not fix this. If everyone uses "wait 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms", everyone still arrives in neat waves at 100, 300 and 700 ms. You need randomness.

### 4. Exponential backoff

**Exponential backoff** doubles the wait after each failure, up to a **cap** (a maximum wait), with a **maximum number of attempts**.

wait = min(cap, base x 2^(attempt - 1))

With base = 100 ms and cap = 5 seconds:

| Attempt that failed | Wait before next try | Total time waited so far |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100 ms | 0.1 s |
| 2 | 200 ms | 0.3 s |
| 3 | 400 ms | 0.7 s |
| 4 | 800 ms | 1.5 s |
| 5 | 1.6 s | 3.1 s |
| 6 | 3.2 s | 6.3 s |
| 7 | 5 s (capped) | 11.3 s |

Early retries are quick, catching short blips. If the problem lasts, retries thin out. The cap stops waits growing absurdly; the attempt limit makes you eventually give up.

A user-facing call with a 2-second target can afford 2 or 3 quick attempts, not 7; background jobs can back off for minutes.

### 5. Jitter: breaking the waves

**Jitter** picks a random wait instead of a fixed one. Two common styles:

- **Full jitter**: wait = random between 0 and the backoff value. For attempt 3, anywhere from 0 to 400 ms.
- **Equal jitter**: wait = half the backoff + random between 0 and the other half. For attempt 3, anywhere from 200 to 400 ms. This keeps a guaranteed minimum wait.

Example: 1,000 clients fail at the same moment. Without jitter, all 1,000 retry at exactly t = 100 ms, a spike of 1,000 requests in one instant. With full jitter, those 1,000 retries spread across 0 to 100 ms, about 10 per millisecond. The total work is similar, but the **peak** is far lower, and the peak is what knocks a service over. Full jitter is a good default; equal jitter suits cases where you want a minimum wait. Both beat no jitter.

### 6. A small code example

```java
long backoffMillis(int attempt) {                     // attempt = 1, 2, 3...
    long base = 100, cap = 5_000;
    long exp = Math.min(cap, base << (attempt - 1));  // 100, 200, 400 ... capped
    return ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(exp + 1); // full jitter: 0..exp
}

<T> T callWithRetry(Supplier<T> call, int maxAttempts) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
        try {
            return call.get();                        // call itself has a timeout
        } catch (TransientException e) {              // 503, timeout, connection reset
            if (attempt >= maxAttempts || !retryBudget.tryAcquire()) throw e;
            Thread.sleep(backoffMillis(attempt));
        }
    }
}
```

In practice, use Resilience4j or your HTTP client, gRPC or mesh retry settings; the logic is the same.

### 7. The other guard rails

- **Retry budgets.** Instead of "3 attempts per request", say "retries may be at most **10% of my traffic**". When things are healthy, the few failures are retried. When a dependency is badly broken, the budget runs out and extra load stays at about 1.1x instead of 3x. Envoy and gRPC support this kind of limit (retry budgets and retry throttling).
- **Retry only what is safe.** Retry reads and idempotent writes. For non-idempotent writes like "place order" or "charge card", send an **idempotency key** so the server can spot a duplicate, or do not retry at all. Remember a timeout does not mean the work failed; it may have succeeded.
- **Retry only transient errors.** Retry 503, 429 (too many requests) and timeouts. Do not retry 400 (bad request) or 404; the answer will not change. If the server sends a **Retry-After** header, obey it.
- **Timeouts and deadlines.** Every call needs a timeout. Better, pass a **deadline** down the chain ("this whole request must finish by 10:00:00.800"), so a lower layer does not retry when the caller has already given up.
- **Circuit breakers.** A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is clearly failing and fails fast for a while, then tests it with a few calls; see the separate answer on circuit breakers for how it works.

## A worked example

**A Flipkart-like product page during a festive sale.**

1. At 8 pm the sale opens. The product page service calls the pricing service, which calls a promotions database. Normal load on pricing is 40,000 RPS; capacity is about 50,000 RPS.
2. A hot promotion row causes lock waits in the database. Pricing replies slow from 30 ms to 900 ms.
3. **Before the fix.** The mobile app retried 3 times, the API gateway retried 3 times, and the product page service retried 3 times, all with a fixed 200 ms wait. Within 20 seconds pricing saw over 150,000 RPS, mostly retries for pages users had already abandoned. The pricing pods ran out of threads, health checks failed, and pods restarted. Every restart brought pods back into a wall of synchronised retries. A 2-minute database hiccup became a **25-minute outage** of product pages.
4. **After the fix**, the team changed four things:
   - Only the product page service retries pricing. The app and gateway fail fast.
   - Retries use exponential backoff with **full jitter** (base 50 ms, cap 1 s, at most 2 attempts), and a **retry budget of 10%**.
   - The product page passes a **deadline** of 800 ms; pricing does not start work on a request that has less than 50 ms left.
   - A **circuit breaker** around pricing falls back to the cached price with a "price may change at checkout" note, and checkout always re-prices.
5. **Next sale, same database hiccup.** Pricing load rises from 40,000 to about 44,000 RPS (the 10% budget), well under capacity. Latency is poor for 2 minutes, a slice of users see cached prices, and the service recovers on its own as soon as the database does. **No outage.**
6. The root cause was the same both times. What decided "blip" versus "outage" was **how callers behaved when things got slow**.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Retries always improve reliability."** They help with brief, random failures. During overload they add load to the thing that is already struggling. Retries need backoff, jitter and a budget.
- **"Backoff alone is enough."** Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together in waves. Randomness is what spreads them out.
- **"More retries at every layer is safer."** Layered retries multiply: 3 layers x 3 attempts is 27x. Retry at one layer and make the rest fail fast.
- **"A timeout means the request failed."** It means you stopped waiting. The server may have finished the work, so retrying a non-idempotent call can create duplicates, like a double charge. Use idempotency keys.
- **"Once the root cause is fixed, the system recovers by itself."** Not if it is in a retry storm. The retry traffic alone can keep it down (a metastable failure). You may need to shed load or open circuit breakers to let it recover.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Retries are dangerous because failures are correlated. When a service slows, all its callers time out at the same time and all of them retry, so the service gets two or three times its normal load exactly when it is weakest. That makes it slower, which causes more retries, and a small slowdown turns into an outage that can outlast the original cause. Layers make it worse: three layers with three attempts each is 27 calls for one user request. I prevent this in a few ways. Exponential backoff, so each retry waits longer, with a cap and an attempt limit. Jitter, a random wait, so clients that failed together do not retry together. A retry budget, so retries are at most around 10% of traffic. I retry at only one layer, only on transient errors, and only for idempotent operations or with an idempotency key. And I pair this with deadlines and a circuit breaker so we fail fast when a dependency is clearly down."*

**Likely follow-ups:**

- *Full jitter or equal jitter?* Full jitter spreads load best and is a good default. Equal jitter keeps a minimum wait, which helps if you never want an instant retry.
- *Which layer should retry?* Usually the one closest to the failing dependency, because it knows best which errors are transient. Upper layers should fail fast and respect the overall deadline.
- *How do you know you have a retry storm?* Compare requests received with unique requests: if the retry ratio jumps from about 1% to 50% or more while latency climbs, retries are feeding the outage. Dashboards should show retry rate separately.

## Key takeaways

- Retries are safe one at a time but dangerous in a crowd, because failures hit **all callers at once**.
- A slow service plus retries creates a **feedback loop**: slower replies, more timeouts, more retries, more load.
- Layered retries **multiply**: 3 layers x 3 attempts = **27x**.
- **Exponential backoff** spreads retries over time; always add a **cap** and an **attempt limit**.
- **Jitter** breaks synchronisation and prevents the **thundering herd**; full jitter is a good default.
- A **retry budget** (about 10% of traffic) puts a hard ceiling on extra load.
- Retry only **transient errors** on **idempotent** operations, at **one layer**, inside a **deadline**.
- Add **circuit breakers** and load shedding so a broken dependency fails fast and can recover.

## Check yourself

1. An app, a gateway and a backend service each make 3 attempts on failure. The database under the backend goes down. How many calls can one user tap generate at the database layer, and what is the fix?
   Answer: Up to 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Retry at only one layer, near the failing dependency, and make the other layers fail fast within a shared deadline.
2. Every client uses backoff of exactly 100, 200 and 400 ms. Why does the service still see big spikes after an outage?
   Answer: Clients that failed at the same moment retry at the same moments, so they arrive in synchronised waves. Adding jitter randomises each wait and spreads the retries out.
3. With base 100 ms, cap 2 s and full jitter, what range can the wait be after the 5th failed attempt?
   Answer: The backoff is min(2000, 100 x 2^4) = 1,600 ms, so with full jitter the wait is anywhere from 0 to 1,600 ms.
4. A "place order" call timed out after 1 second. Should the client simply retry it?
   Answer: Not blindly. The order may have been created even though the reply was lost. Retry only with an idempotency key so the server returns the original order instead of creating a duplicate.

question: How does Git actually remember every version of your code without filling your disk, and what really happens in a commit, a branch and a merge?
answer:
## The short answer

Git is a small **database of snapshots**. Every time you commit, Git records what your **whole project looks like** at that moment, not a list of changes. That sounds wasteful, but it isn't, for three reasons:

- **Every piece of content is named by its fingerprint (hash).** If a file did not change, its fingerprint did not change, so Git simply points at the copy it already has. **Identical content is stored once**, no matter how many commits or folders use it.
- **Everything is compressed.** Each stored object is zlib-compressed, and from time to time Git packs objects into **packfiles**, where similar versions of a file are stored as small **deltas** (differences) against each other.
- **Commits, branches and merges are tiny.** A commit is a short text record pointing to a snapshot and its parent. A **branch is just a file holding one 40-character hash**. A merge is a commit with two parents.

## The intuition

Think of a **family photo album**. Each page is a full photo of the family on one day: that is a **snapshot**. You never store "Ravi got a haircut" as a note; you just take a new photo. Flipping to any page shows you the whole family as it was.

Now imagine the album is clever. If grandma looks exactly the same as in the last photo, it reuses the same cut-out of her; only people who changed get new cut-outs. That is Git: **unchanged files are reused, changed files get a new copy**.

A few terms, defined once:

- **Repository (repo)**: the project folder plus its hidden `.git` folder, where all history lives.
- **Hash**: a fixed-length fingerprint computed from content. Git uses **SHA-1** by default (40 hexadecimal characters); newer Git can also use SHA-256. Change one byte of content and the hash changes completely.
- **Object**: one stored item in Git's database. There are four kinds: **blob**, **tree**, **commit** and **tag**.
- **Content-addressed**: an object's name *is* the hash of its content. You find things by "what they are", not "where they are".
- **Ref**: a name (like `main`) that points to a commit hash. Branches and tags are refs.
- **HEAD**: Git's "you are here" marker: which branch (or commit) you currently have checked out.

## How it actually works

### 1. Snapshots, not diffs

Older tools like CVS and Subversion stored **diffs**: version 5 = version 1 plus four sets of changes. Git stores **snapshots** and computes diffs on the fly, so checking out any old version is fast and branches are cheap.

### 2. The three main objects

- **Blob** (binary large object): the raw bytes of one file. No file name, no permissions, just content.
- **Tree**: one directory listing. Each line says: mode, type, hash, name. For example, "100644 blob a1b2... `Cart.java`" and "040000 tree c3d4... `payments`". A tree can point to blobs (files) and to other trees (subfolders).
- **Commit**: a small text record containing the **top-level tree hash**, the **parent commit hash(es)**, the author, the committer, timestamps and the message.

A real commit object looks roughly like this:

```
tree 9c1f4e0a...           (snapshot of the whole project)
parent 4b7d22e1...         (the commit before this one)
author Asha <asha@example.com> 1760500000 +0530
committer Asha <asha@example.com> 1760500000 +0530

Add UPI retry on timeout
```

### 3. Named by hash

An object's name is the hash of a short header plus its content. For a blob it is `SHA-1("blob " + size + "\0" + content)`. You can see this yourself:

```
$ echo 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
```

The same calculation in Java:

```java
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.HexFormat;

public class BlobHash {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        byte[] content = "hello\n".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        byte[] header = ("blob " + content.length + "\0").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        MessageDigest sha1 = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1");
        sha1.update(header);
        sha1.update(content);
        System.out.println(HexFormat.of().formatHex(sha1.digest()));
        // prints ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
    }
}
```

Git stores this object at `.git/objects/ce/013625...` (first two characters become a folder name, to keep folders small).

Two big consequences:

- **Deduplication for free.** If 30 commits contain the same `README.md`, there is exactly one blob for it. If you copy a file into two folders, there is still one blob. A tree whose files did not change keeps the same hash, so a commit that touches one file in a 10,000-file project creates only **one new blob plus the few trees on the path to it** (say, 4 or 5 trees), and reuses everything else.
- **Tamper evidence.** A commit hash covers its tree (and so every blob) and its parent. Change any byte in history and every later hash changes, so a commit hash identifies **the entire history leading to it**.

### 4. Compression and packfiles

New objects are **loose objects**: one zlib-compressed file each. Source code often compresses to a third of its size or less. During `git gc` (also run automatically now and then) and when pushing or fetching, Git builds a **packfile**: one big file of many objects plus an index. Inside it, similar objects (often successive versions of one file) are stored as one full copy plus **deltas**, usually keeping the **newest** version whole because you read it most.

So Git does use differences, but only as a **storage trick under the hood**; the model is always "full snapshot per commit". The exception is **large binaries** (videos, ML model weights): they compress and delta poorly, which is why Git LFS exists.

### 5. A commit, step by step

When you run `git add` and `git commit`:

1. `git add Cart.java` hashes the file, writes a blob if it is new, and records it in the **index** (also called the **staging area**: a file listing exactly what the next snapshot will contain).
2. `git commit` turns the index into tree objects, reusing every tree whose hash is unchanged.
3. It writes a commit object pointing to the new top tree and to the current commit as parent.
4. It moves the current branch to the new commit's hash. That is all.

### 6. A branch is a movable label

A branch is a tiny file. `.git/refs/heads/main` contains one line: a commit hash. `git branch feature/coupons` writes a **new 41-byte file** (40 hex characters plus a newline). No files are copied. Committing on that branch just rewrites the file with the new hash.

### 7. HEAD: you are here

`.git/HEAD` normally contains `ref: refs/heads/main`, meaning "I am on main". `git switch feature/coupons` rewrites HEAD to point at that branch and updates your working files to match its snapshot. If you check out a commit hash directly, HEAD holds the hash itself: this is **detached HEAD**. New commits made there are not on any branch, so they are easy to lose unless you create a branch for them.

### 8. Merge: fast-forward vs three-way

Here is a typical picture. `main` and `feature` split after commit B:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[A first commit] --> B[B merge base]
    B --> C[C on main]
    B --> D[D on feature]
    D --> E[E on feature]
    C --> M[M merge commit]
    E --> M
    MAIN[main label] -.-> M
    FEAT[feature label] -.-> E
    HEAD[HEAD] -.-> MAIN
```

(Arrows run from older to newer for readability; inside Git, each commit actually stores a pointer back to its parent.)

- **Fast-forward merge**: if `main` has not moved since `feature` branched off, then `feature` already contains everything in `main`. Git just **slides the `main` label forward** to the feature's latest commit. No new commit is created.
- **Three-way merge**: if both sides moved (C on main, D and E on feature), Git finds the **merge base**, the best common ancestor (B here). It compares three snapshots: base B, "ours" C and "theirs" E. For each file and each region: if only one side changed it, take that change; if neither changed it, keep it; if **both changed the same lines differently**, that is a **conflict**. If all goes well, Git writes a **merge commit** M with **two parents** (C and E).

### 9. Conflicts

A conflict is not an error; it is Git saying "two people changed the same spot and I will not guess". Git writes both versions into the file with markers:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
int maxRetries = 3;
=======
int maxRetries = 5;
>>>>>>> feature/upi-retry
```

You edit the file to the right result, `git add` it, and `git commit` to finish. Git merges by **lines of text**, not meaning, so a clean merge can still be logically wrong (one branch renames a method, the other adds a new call to the old name). That is why CI tests still run after a merge.

### 10. Rebase in one paragraph

**Rebase** is the other way to combine work. Instead of creating a merge commit, `git rebase main` (run on `feature`) takes the feature's commits (D and E), and **replays** each one on top of the latest `main`, creating new commits D' and E'. The changes are the same, but the parents differ, so the **hashes are new**: these are new commits, and the old D and E are abandoned. The result is a straight, tidy history, as if you had started your work from the latest main. The cost is that you have rewritten history.

### 11. Why rewriting shared history is risky

Rebase, `commit --amend`, and `reset` followed by `push --force` all replace commits with new ones. If you are the only person who has those commits, that is fine. But if teammates already built on the old D and E, their history now disagrees with the server: duplicate commits, painful conflicts, or, after a careless force-push, **work silently vanishing from the shared branch**. Common rules: **rebase only private branches**, never force-push `main`, use `--force-with-lease` (refuses if the remote moved), and protect key branches. Locally, `git reflog` lists where HEAD has been, so "lost" commits can usually be recovered for some weeks.

## A worked example

Take a Flipkart-like checkout service with about 5,000 files.

1. **Monday.** Main is at commit B. Asha creates `feature/upi-retry` with `git switch -c feature/upi-retry`. Git writes one tiny ref file and updates HEAD. Nothing is copied.
2. She edits `PaymentClient.java` in `src/main/java/com/shop/payments/` and commits. Git writes **1 new blob**, about **6 new trees** (one for each folder on the path, up to the root) and **1 commit**. The other 4,999 file blobs and all untouched folders are reused by hash. The new commit is D.
3. **Tuesday.** She commits a test change: commit E. Meanwhile Ravi merges a coupon fix into main: commit C, which changes `CouponService.java` and, unluckily, the same `maxRetries` line in `PaymentConfig.java`.
4. **Wednesday.** Asha runs `git switch main`, `git pull`, then `git merge feature/upi-retry`. Main has moved, so a fast-forward is impossible. Git finds merge base B and does a three-way merge. `CouponService.java` changed only on main: taken automatically. `PaymentClient.java` changed only on the feature: taken automatically. `PaymentConfig.java` changed on both sides in the same line: **conflict**.
5. Asha and Ravi agree the value should be 3 with backoff. She edits the file, removes the markers, runs `git add` and `git commit`. Git creates merge commit M with parents C and E. CI runs the full test suite on M before it is deployed for the festive sale.
6. **Thursday.** Kiran rebases a shared release branch and force-pushes. Two teammates who built on the old commits now see duplicates. The team recovers via `git reflog` and turns on **branch protection** against force-pushes.
7. After a year and 40,000 commits, shared objects and packfiles keep `.git` manageable, not "40,000 copies of the project".

## Common misconceptions

- **"Git stores diffs."** The model is full snapshots. Diffs are computed when you ask. Deltas exist only inside packfiles, purely to save space.
- **"A branch is a copy of the code."** A branch is a 41-byte file holding one commit hash. Creating 100 branches costs almost nothing.
- **"Snapshots must waste huge disk space."** Unchanged files and folders share the same objects by hash, everything is compressed, and packfiles delta-compress similar versions. Large binaries are the real exception.
- **"A merge conflict means something broke."** It means both sides changed the same lines and Git refuses to guess. Equally, a clean merge does not prove the code is correct; Git merges text, not meaning.
- **"Rebase just moves my commits."** It creates **new commits with new hashes**. The old ones remain until garbage-collected. That is exactly why rebasing shared commits causes trouble.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Git is a content-addressed database of snapshots. Each file's content is stored as a blob, each directory as a tree, and each commit is a small record pointing to the top-level tree, its parent commits, the author and the message. Every object is named by the hash of its content, so identical content is stored once: when I change one file in a big project, a commit adds one blob, a few trees for the path, and the commit itself, and reuses everything else. Objects are zlib-compressed and periodically packed into packfiles with delta compression, so diffs exist only as a storage optimisation. A branch is just a file holding a commit hash, and HEAD says which branch I am on, so branching is nearly free. A merge is fast-forward if only one side moved, otherwise a three-way merge against the merge base, producing a commit with two parents; conflicts happen when both sides changed the same lines. Rebase replays commits on a new base, creating new hashes, which is why I only rebase private branches and never force-push shared ones."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *Merge or rebase: which do you prefer?* It depends on the team. Rebase keeps feature branches tidy before review; merge keeps an honest record of when work joined. A common rule: rebase your own branch locally, then merge (or squash-merge) into main through a pull request.
- *How do you handle large binary files?* Keep them out of normal Git history; use Git LFS or an artifact store, because binaries compress and delta poorly and bloat every clone.

## Key takeaways

- Git stores **snapshots**, not diffs; diffs are computed on demand.
- Objects are **blobs** (file content), **trees** (directories) and **commits** (snapshot plus parents plus metadata), all **named by their hash**.
- **Identical content is stored once**; a commit only adds what actually changed.
- **zlib compression and packfiles** with deltas keep the repository small.
- A **branch is a movable label**: a tiny file with one commit hash. **HEAD** marks where you are.
- **Fast-forward** just moves a label; a **three-way merge** uses the merge base and creates a two-parent commit.
- **Conflicts** mean both sides changed the same lines; resolve, add, commit, and still run tests.
- **Rebase creates new commits**; never rewrite history others have already pulled.

## Check yourself

1. You change one file in a project of 2,000 files and commit. Roughly what new objects does Git create?
   Answer: One new blob for the changed file, one new tree for each folder on the path from that file up to the root, and one commit object. Every other blob and tree is reused because its hash did not change.
2. What is actually inside `.git/refs/heads/main`, and what happens to it when you commit on main?
   Answer: A single commit hash (40 hex characters plus a newline). After a commit, Git overwrites it with the new commit's hash, moving the label forward.
3. When does Git do a fast-forward merge instead of a three-way merge?
   Answer: When the branch you merge into has no commits that the other branch lacks, so its tip is an ancestor of the other tip. Git just moves the label forward. If both sides have new commits, it does a three-way merge using the merge base and creates a merge commit with two parents.
4. Why is rebasing a branch that teammates have already pulled risky?
   Answer: Rebase replaces the commits with new ones that have different hashes. Teammates' work is built on the old commits, so their history diverges from the server, causing duplicate commits and conflicts, and a careless force-push can drop their work from the shared branch.

question: How does a shopping app decide what to show in "Customers who bought this also bought" and "Recommended for you"?
answer:
## The short answer

These two widgets are powered by a **recommendation system**: software that guesses which products a person is most likely to want next. They use slightly different signals:

- **"Customers who bought this also bought"** is mostly **item-to-item**: for the product on screen, it looks up which other products are most often bought by the same people. It is about the *product*, not about you.
- **"Recommended for you"** is **personalised**: it uses *your* history (views, searches, cart adds, purchases) to find products that people with similar behaviour liked, or that look like things you liked.

At scale, both are built as a **two-stage system**:

1. **Candidate generation**: quickly pull a few hundred possibly-relevant products out of crores (tens of millions) using cheap methods such as co-purchase counts, **collaborative filtering** and **embeddings**.
2. **Ranking**: a machine-learning model scores each candidate on "how likely is this user to click or buy this, right now?" using many features, then business rules remove bad results (things you already bought, out-of-stock items, ten near-identical phone cases).

Most heavy work is **precomputed offline** (overnight or hourly batch jobs); a thin **real-time** layer adjusts for what you did in the last few minutes. Quality is judged offline with metrics like **precision@k**, and finally by **A/B tests** on click-through rate and conversion.

## The intuition

Think of an experienced shopkeeper at a kirana store near your home.

- When you buy **Maggi**, he says, "Many people who take Maggi also take a **Tata Salt** packet and eggs." He is not thinking about you; he just remembers what usually goes together in the same basket. That is **"Customers who bought this also bought"**.
- When you walk in, he says, "Sir, the new **filter coffee powder** came in. People who buy what you buy liked it." He remembers *your* habits and what *customers like you* buy. That is **"Recommended for you"**.
- He also knows the shop: "You liked this Bru coffee, this one is similar, also South Indian style." That is matching by **product attributes**.
- He does not suggest the bread you bought an hour ago, or push salt on everyone just because it sells most.

A recommendation system is that shopkeeper's memory, written down as numbers, for 50 crore customers at once.

Terms used below:
- **Interaction**: any signal a user gives about an item: view, click, add to cart, purchase, rating, return.
- **Item-to-item**: "items similar to this item", computed from who bought them together.
- **Collaborative filtering (CF)**: recommending from the behaviour of *other similar users*, without needing to understand what the product is.
