Because the register is sorted by date, the librarian opens it right at that spot (like using a book's index) and reads 20. New books added at the top do not move your bookmark.

Terms used below:
- **Page size / LIMIT**: how many rows to return per page (here 20).
- **OFFSET**: how many rows to skip before returning results.
- **Index**: a sorted lookup structure (usually a **B-tree**) that lets the database find a value quickly without scanning the whole table.
- **Cursor / keyset**: the sort values of the last row you saw, used as the starting point for the next page.
- **Opaque token**: a cursor packed into a string the client should not read or edit, like `eyJjIjoiMjAyNi0...`.
- **Stable sort / tie-breaker**: a sort order where no two rows are equal, usually by adding the unique `id` as the last sort column.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why OFFSET is slow: read and throw away

Take an `orders` table with an index on `(user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`. One heavy buyer has 100,000 orders.

```sql
-- page 1
SELECT id, created_at, total FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;

-- page 5,000
SELECT id, created_at, total FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 99980;
```

The index finds where user 42's orders start very quickly. But an index has **no idea what "row number 99,981" is**. A B-tree can find a **value** fast; it cannot find a **position** fast. So the database walks the index entries in order, counting, and discards the first 99,980.

| Page | OFFSET | Rows walked | Rows returned |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 20 | 20 |
| 50 | 980 | 1,000 | 20 |
| 500 | 9,980 | 10,000 | 20 |
| 5,000 | 99,980 | 100,000 | 20 |

The work grows in **direct proportion to the page number**. If the query needs columns not in the index, many engines also fetch the full row for every skipped entry. Exact timings depend on the engine and caching, but the shape is always the same: page 1 in a millisecond or two, page 5,000 in hundreds of milliseconds or more.

### 2. Why OFFSET repeats and skips items

OFFSET is a **position**, and positions move when the list changes between two requests.

- You load page 1 (orders 1 to 20). A new order is placed. You load page 2 with OFFSET 20. The old order #20 is now at position 21, so it appears again: **duplicate**.
- You load page 1. Order #5 is deleted or hidden (for example, archived). Everything moves up one. Page 2 with OFFSET 20 now starts at what used to be #22. Old #21 is **never shown**.

### 3. Cursor (keyset) pagination: seek, then read

Instead of "skip N," you remember the **sort values of the last row** and ask for rows **after** them:

```sql
-- first page: no cursor
SELECT id, created_at, total FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- next page: last row seen was (2026-10-14 10:42:07, 88123)
SELECT id, created_at, total FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
  AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-14 10:42:07', 88123)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

With the index on `(user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`, the database **seeks** straight to that point in the B-tree (a few page reads, roughly log of the table size) and reads the next 20 entries. **Cost per page stays flat**, whether it is page 2 or page 5,000.

Three details that matter:

- **Tie-breaker.** Many orders can share the same `created_at` to the second. If you sort only by `created_at`, rows with equal timestamps can be skipped or repeated at page edges. Adding the unique `id` makes the order **total** (no ties).
- **Row-value comparison.** `(created_at, id) < (x, y)` means "created earlier, or same time with a smaller id." Some engines use the index better with the expanded form `created_at < x OR (created_at = x AND id < y)`; check the plan with `EXPLAIN`.
- **Index must match the sort.** The `WHERE` filter plus the `ORDER BY` columns, in the same order and direction, must be an index prefix. Otherwise the database sorts everything first and you lose the benefit.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Client asks next page] --> B{Has cursor}
  B -- no --> C[Read first 20 rows]
  B -- yes --> D[Decode cursor token]
  D --> E[Seek index to last row]
  E --> F[Read next 20 rows]
  C --> G[Build next cursor]
  F --> G
  G --> H[Return items and cursor]
```

### 4. Cursors in an API: make them opaque

Wrap the cursor in an **opaque token**:

```json
GET /v1/orders?limit=20
{
  "items": [ ... 20 orders ... ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJjIjoiMjAyNi0xMC0xNFQxMDo0MjowNyIsImkiOjg4MTIzfQ",
  "has_more": true
}

GET /v1/orders?limit=20&cursor=eyJjIjoiMjAyNi0xMC0xNFQxMDo0MjowNyIsImkiOjg4MTIzfQ
```

Inside, the token is just `{"c":"2026-10-14T10:42:07","i":88123}`, Base64-encoded. Opaque means you can **change the sort or storage later** without breaking clients, and you can **sign** it (an HMAC, a keyed checksum) so it cannot be tampered with. A small Java sketch:

```java
record Cursor(Instant createdAt, long id) {
    String encode() {
        String raw = createdAt.toString() + "|" + id;
        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()
                     .encodeToString(raw.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    }
    static Cursor decode(String token) {
        String raw = new String(Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(token), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        String[] p = raw.split("\\|");
        return new Cursor(Instant.parse(p[0]), Long.parseLong(p[1]));
    }
}
```

For `has_more`, fetch **21 rows** and return 20; a 21st means another page exists.

### 5. The trade-offs

| | Offset | Cursor / keyset |
|---|---|---|
| Speed on deep pages | Gets slower with every page | Flat |
| Jump to page N | Yes | No, only next (and previous) |
| Duplicates or skips on changing data | Yes | No for inserts and deletes elsewhere |
| Sort by any column | Easy | Needs a unique, indexed sort key |
| Total count | Usually shown | Usually not shown |
| Best for | Small admin tables, reports | Feeds, infinite scroll, APIs, exports |

**Total counts** are a separate cost. `SELECT COUNT(*)` over 100,000 rows still walks 100,000 index entries, on every request. Common answers: do not show it, show "1,000+" (count with a cap), cache it, or keep a counter updated on writes.

**Changing sort values.** If a row's sort value changes (price, ranking score), it can still move across your cursor; ranked feeds often paginate over a **snapshot** of ordered IDs.

### 6. Infinite scroll

Infinite scroll is the perfect match for cursors: the user only ever asks for "more," never "page 317." The app keeps `next_cursor`, fetches the next batch near the bottom, and **de-duplicates by id** as a safety net. If product insists on page numbers, use offset for the first few pages and **cap the depth**.

## A worked example

**"My Orders" in a Flipkart-like app during the festive sale.**

1. The old design: `GET /orders?page=N&size=20`, implemented with `LIMIT 20 OFFSET (N-1)*20`, plus a `COUNT(*)` for "Page 3 of 612." For most users with 30 orders, this is fine.
2. A reseller account has 120,000 orders. Their support tool loads page 5,000. The query walks about 100,000 index entries and fetches rows for each. It takes 2 seconds and burns database CPU. An internal script that exports all orders page by page does this 6,000 times: the total work is roughly 6,000 x 60,000 average rows, about **360 million row reads** to export 120,000 orders.
3. Meanwhile, a customer scrolls "My Orders" while a new order arrives; the last order of page 1 repeats on page 2. Another hides an order mid-scroll, and one order silently vanishes. Support tickets: "my order is missing."
4. The fix. Add an index on `(user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`. Change the API to `GET /orders?limit=20&cursor=...` returning `next_cursor`. The app switches to infinite scroll. The query becomes the keyset version from section 3.
5. Results. Every page reads about 20 index entries. The export script now does 6,000 requests of about 20 rows each, about **120,000 row reads**, roughly 3,000 times less work. Page 5,000 for the reseller takes as long as page 1, a few milliseconds.
6. New orders arriving at the top no longer shift anything: the cursor says "older than order 88123," and that does not change. No more duplicates. Deleted orders simply are not returned; nothing else moves.
7. The trade-off: "Page 3 of 612" is gone. A date filter ("Orders from 2024") lets people jump back in time, and it is just another starting point for the seek.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Adding an index fixes slow OFFSET."** An index helps find the start and avoid sorting, but it cannot skip to a position. The database still walks every skipped entry. Only a seek on values (keyset) avoids that.
- **"Cursor pagination means a database cursor."** No. API cursor pagination is **stateless**: the cursor is just the last row's sort values, sent back by the client.
- **"Sorting by created_at alone is enough."** Timestamps tie. Without a unique tie-breaker like `id`, rows at page edges can be skipped or repeated, even with keyset.
- **"Cursors make the list a perfect snapshot."** They fix shifts from inserts and deletes, but if the sort value of a row changes (score, price), it can still move across your cursor. Use a snapshot if that matters.
- **"Offset is always bad."** For small tables and the first few pages it is fine. The problem is **deep pages on large or changing data**.
- **"We need the total count for good UX."** Users rarely need "12,384 results" exactly. "1,000+" or no count at all is usually fine, and far cheaper.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Offset pagination, LIMIT 20 OFFSET N, asks the database to skip N rows. A B-tree index can find a value quickly but not a position, so the database walks and throws away all N rows. Page 1 reads 20 rows; page 5,000 reads 100,000. It also counts positions in a changing list, so a new row at the top makes the next page repeat an item, and a deleted row makes one get skipped. Cursor, or keyset, pagination remembers the sort values of the last row I returned, say created_at and id, and the next query is WHERE (created_at, id) less than those values, ORDER BY created_at, id, LIMIT 20. With an index on exactly those columns, the database seeks straight there, so every page costs the same and inserts do not shift anything. In an API I return that as an opaque, signed next_cursor token. The trade-offs: no jumping to page N, the sort key must be unique and indexed, and I avoid exact total counts. For feeds, infinite scroll and exports I use cursors; for small admin tables offset is fine."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *How do you support "previous page"?* Flip the comparison and sort direction (`>` and `ORDER BY ... ASC`), take 20, then reverse them before returning. Return both `next_cursor` and `prev_cursor`.
- *What if users sort by price?* Use `(price, id)` as the key and add an index on `(category_id, price, id)`. If prices change during browsing, items may move; accept it, or paginate over a snapshot of IDs.
- *How do you show "Page 3 of 612"?* Usually you don't. Show "1,000+," cache the count, or keep a counter. If page numbers are a hard requirement, use offset only for the first few pages and cap the depth.

## Key takeaways

- **OFFSET reads and discards** every skipped row; cost grows with the page number.
- OFFSET counts **positions**, so inserts and deletes cause **duplicates and skips**.
- **Keyset/cursor pagination** seeks to the last seen value: `WHERE (created_at, id) < (...) ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20`.
- It needs an **index matching the filter and sort**, and a **unique tie-breaker** like `id`.
- In APIs, return an **opaque, signed `next_cursor`**, and fetch limit+1 to know `has_more`.
- Trade-offs: **no jumping to page N**, and **total counts are expensive**; avoid or cap them.
- Cursors suit **infinite scroll, feeds and bulk exports**; offset is fine for small, stable lists.

## Check yourself

1. A query uses `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000` on an indexed column. Why is it still slow?
   Answer: The index lets the database find values fast, not row positions, so it must walk 200,000 index entries (and often fetch their rows) and throw them away before returning 20.
2. A user loads page 1 of a feed with offset pagination, then 3 new posts are added at the top before they load page 2. What do they see?
   Answer: The last 3 posts of page 1 appear again at the start of page 2, because every item moved down 3 positions. With a cursor, page 2 starts after the last seen post, so nothing repeats.
3. Why does the keyset query compare `(created_at, id)` and not just `created_at`?
   Answer: Several rows can share the same timestamp. Adding the unique id makes the sort order total, so rows with equal timestamps at a page boundary are neither skipped nor repeated.
4. Product wants a "jump to page 400" box on an infinite-scroll order list. What do you propose?
   Answer: Explain that cursors cannot jump to a position cheaply. Offer a filter that sets a starting value instead, such as a date ("orders from March 2024"), which is also a fast index seek, or allow offset only for the first few pages with a depth cap.
title: Offset vs cursor pagination

question: When a seller uploads 10 product photos, how does the app store them and show fast, small versions on every phone? How do image upload pipelines work?
answer: ## The short answer When a seller uploads 10 product photos, a well-built app does **not** push them through its own servers or save them in its database. Instead: 1. The app asks the backend for **pre-signed upload URLs**: short-lived, one-time "permission slips" that let the phone upload each file **straight to object storage** (an S3-like store built for big files). 2. The database stores only a small row per photo: an **ID**, the **storage key** (the file's name inside the store), a **status** and some metadata. Not the image bytes. 3. When an upload finishes, a message goes onto a **queue**. **Background workers** pick it up and **validate** the file, **strip hidden metadata** (like GPS location), **check it for unsafe content**, and **resize** it into several sizes (thumbnail, listing card, zoom view), each saved as **WebP or AVIF**, modern formats that are much smaller than JPEG for the same quality. 4. Shoppers' phones load these images from a **CDN** (content delivery network: servers in many cities that keep copies close to users), using **versioned URLs** so they can be cached for a very long time. 5. The page uses **responsive images** (`srcset`), so a cheap phone on 4G downloads a 30 KB image, not a 4 MB original. Two extra pieces keep it healthy: **lifecycle rules** that move or delete old files to control storage cost, and **idempotent retries** so a failed step can safely run again. ## The intuition Think of a **photo studio with a big back-room warehouse**. - The **front desk** (your API server) is small and busy. You don't want customers carrying heavy boxes through it. So the desk hands each customer a **numbered token** that lets them drop their box **directly at the warehouse door** for the next 15 minutes. That token is the **pre-signed URL**. - The front desk keeps only a **register** (the database): "box 42 belongs to seller S9, received, not yet processed". It doesn't keep the boxes themselves. - In the back, **workers** take boxes off a **conveyor belt** (the queue). They check the box isn't empty or dangerous, peel off private labels, and make **several prints in different sizes**: passport size, postcard size, poster size. - The prints go to **kiosks in every neighbourhood** (the CDN), so customers pick them up nearby. Terms used below: - **Object storage**: a service (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, MinIO) that stores files ("objects") by a **key**, like `originals/9f2c`. Cheap, almost unlimited, very durable. - **Pre-signed URL**: a URL with a **cryptographic signature** and an **expiry time** baked in. Anyone holding it can do exactly one allowed action (like "PUT this key") until it expires. - **Queue**: a list of jobs waiting to be done (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ). - **Variant**: one processed version of an image, like the 400-pixel-wide WebP. - **Idempotent**: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. ## How it actually works ### 1. Why not store images in the database? You *can* put image bytes in a database column (a BLOB, "binary large object"). It works for a small app. At scale it hurts: - **Size**: a phone photo is 3-6 MB; a million products with 8 photos each is roughly 30 TB. Database storage is expensive per GB and slow to back up and replicate. - **Wrong tool for serving**: every image view would hit the database. Object storage plus a CDN is built for billions of file reads. So the rule is: **bytes in object storage, facts in the database**. ### 2. Keys and layout Object storage has no real folders; a key is just a string. A common layout: ``` originals/{imageId} -- private, never served directly variants/{imageId}/v{version}/w400.webp variants/{imageId}/v{version}/w800.avif ``` Use a **random ID** (like a UUID) instead of the seller's filename, which can clash ("IMG_0001.jpg") or leak information. ### 3. Pre-signed upload URLs: files go straight to storage ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant P as Seller app participant A as API participant S as Object storage participant Q as Queue P->>A: I want to upload 10 photos A->>A: check seller, create 10 rows status PENDING A-->>P: 10 pre-signed PUT URLs, valid 15 min P->>S: PUT photo bytes directly S->>Q: upload complete event P->>A: confirm upload, optional ``` Why this is better than uploading through your API: - Your API servers never hold 50 MB of photos per seller; they only sign URLs. - Storage supports **multipart upload** (split a big file into parts, retry only the failed part), which matters on patchy mobile networks. - You can put **limits inside the signature**: content type, maximum size (via a signed POST policy), exact key, short expiry. A simplified Java sketch with the AWS SDK v2: ```java PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder() .bucket("seller-uploads") .key("originals/" + imageId) .contentType("image/jpeg") .build(); PresignedPutObjectRequest signed = presigner.presignPutObject(r -> r .signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(15)) .putObjectRequest(put)); return signed.url().toString(); // give this to the phone ``` The upload bucket stays **private**. Nobody can read originals from the internet. ### 4. Background processing through a queue When storage reports "object created" (or the app calls a confirm endpoint), a job goes on the queue. Workers do the heavy lifting **asynchronously**, meaning the seller doesn't wait for it. ```mermaid flowchart TD U[Original uploaded] --> Q[Queue job] Q --> V[Validate file] V --> M[Strip metadata] M --> C[Moderation check] C --> R[Resize to sizes] R --> E[Encode WebP and AVIF] E --> W[Write variants] W --> D[Mark READY in DB] C --> X[Reject and notify] ``` Each step, in plain terms: - **Validate**: don't trust the file extension. Read the first bytes (the "magic number") to confirm it really is JPEG, PNG or HEIC. Enforce size and pixel limits (say 50 megapixels) to block **decompression bombs**: tiny files that expand into enormous images. Run the image library in an isolated container, because image parsers have had security bugs. - **Strip metadata**: phone photos carry **EXIF** data (camera, time, sometimes GPS location). Remove it, but first apply the **orientation** tag, or photos appear sideways. - **Moderation**: automated checks for nudity, violence, prohibited items or text overlays like phone numbers. Unclear cases go to a **human review queue**. - **Resize**: a fixed set of widths, for example 150 (thumbnail), 400 (listing grid), 800 (product page), 1600 (zoom), keeping the aspect ratio. - **Encode**: **WebP** is typically 25-35% smaller than JPEG at similar quality; **AVIF** is often smaller still but slower to encode. Keep a JPEG fallback. - **Write and publish**: write variants under a new **version** path, then update the database row to `READY` with the version number. Only then does the product page start using them. Rough numbers: one 4 MB photo becomes about 12 KB (thumbnail), 35 KB (400 px), 90 KB (800 px) and 250 KB (1600 px), costing roughly 0.5-2 seconds of CPU. That is why it runs on workers that **scale with queue length**, not in the request. ### 5. CDN delivery with versioned URLs Shoppers never read from storage directly. The URL points at a CDN: ``` https://img.example-cdn.com/variants/9f2c/v3/w400.webp ``` Because **the version is in the URL**, the file at that URL never changes. So the CDN and the phone can cache it with: ``` Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable ``` One year, and "immutable" means the browser won't even ask whether it changed. When the seller replaces a photo, you write `v4` and point the product at the new URL. No CDN **purge** (forced deletion of cached copies) is needed; old copies simply stop being requested. The CDN reads storage only on a **cache miss**, and the bucket is locked so only the CDN can read it. ### 6. Responsive images: the right size for each phone A budget phone with a 360-pixel-wide screen does not need the 1600-pixel image. HTML lets the browser choose: ``` ``` - `srcset` lists the available files and their widths. - `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will be on screen, so it can pick the smallest file that still looks sharp (it accounts for screen pixel density). - `` with `` lets browsers that support AVIF get it, others fall back to WebP or JPEG. - `loading="lazy"` delays off-screen images. Native apps do the same in code: request the variant matching the view size and screen density. ### 7. Storage cost and lifecycle rules Storage is cheap per GB but grows forever if you let it. **Lifecycle rules** are policies on the bucket that act automatically by age or prefix: - **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after 1 day (half-finished uploads otherwise cost money silently). - **Delete abandoned uploads** still `PENDING` after 24 hours. - Move **originals** to a cheaper **storage class** (infrequent access or archive) after 30-90 days; they're kept only to regenerate variants. - Delete **old versions** of variants some days after they are replaced. CDN **egress** (data sent to users) often costs more than storage, another reason small files pay off. ### 8. Retries and idempotency Things fail: a worker crashes mid-resize, the queue delivers a message twice, a phone retries an upload on a flaky connection. Make every step safe to repeat: - **Deterministic output keys**: the worker always writes `variants/{imageId}/v{version}/w400.webp`. Running twice just overwrites the same file with the same bytes. - **Conditional status update**: `UPDATE images SET status='READY' WHERE id=? AND version=? AND status='PROCESSING'`. A duplicate job changes nothing. - **Idempotency key on "create upload"**: if the app retries the request, return the same image IDs instead of creating 20 rows. - **Retry with backoff**, then a **dead-letter queue** (a parking area for jobs that keep failing) with an alert, so one corrupt file doesn't block the line. ## A worked example **A seller on a Flipkart-like marketplace lists a new kurta with 10 photos, during the run-up to a big festive sale.** 1. She picks 10 photos (3-5 MB each, some HEIC from an iPhone). The app calls `POST /uploads` with the count, file types and an idempotency key. 2. The API checks she is a verified seller under her daily quota, creates 10 rows (`status=PENDING`, random IDs), and returns 10 pre-signed PUT URLs valid for 15 minutes, each locked to one key, `image/*`, max 20 MB. 3. The app uploads 3 at a time directly to the storage bucket. Photo 7 fails halfway on a weak signal; the app retries only that file with the same URL. The API never touches the 40 MB. 4. Each completed upload puts a job on the queue. With the sale-time backlog, autoscaling has raised workers from 50 to 300. 5. A worker takes photo 1: magic bytes say HEIC, size fine. It rotates per EXIF, strips EXIF (which contained GPS coordinates), runs moderation (clean), makes 150/400/800/1600 px versions in WebP and AVIF plus a JPEG fallback, writes them under `v1/`, and sets the row to `READY`. About 2 seconds of work. 6. Photo 9 has her phone number printed on it. Moderation rejects it and she sees "Photo 9 rejected: remove contact details". The other 9 go live. 7. A shopper in a small town opens the listing on a budget Android phone. The grid card requests the `w400.webp` (35 KB) from the nearest CDN edge. On the product page, `srcset` picks the 800 px image. Pinch-to-zoom loads the 1600 px one only then. 8. Next week she replaces photo 3. The pipeline writes `v2/`, the product points at the new URLs, and phones see the new photo on the next page load, with no purge. A lifecycle rule deletes `v1/` 30 days later. ## Common misconceptions - **"Just upload to our API server and let it save the file."** That puts big, slow uploads on your most precious servers and ties up threads and memory. Pre-signed URLs send bytes directly to storage while your API keeps control through what it signs. - **"A pre-signed URL is a security hole."** It allows one action on one key for a few minutes. You still validate the file afterwards because the client controls the bytes. - **"Purge the CDN whenever an image changes."** Purges are slow, rate-limited and easy to miss. **Versioned URLs** make changes instant and allow year-long caching. - **"Serve the biggest image and let CSS shrink it."** The phone still downloads all the bytes. That wastes data, battery and time. Use `srcset` and sized variants. - **"Storage is cheap, so keep everything."** Abandoned uploads, half-finished multipart parts and old versions add up to terabytes. Lifecycle rules handle it automatically; egress is often the bigger cost anyway. ## How to say it in an interview *"I keep image bytes out of the database and out of my API servers. The app asks the API for pre-signed upload URLs, which are short-lived, signed permission to put one file at one key in object storage. The phone uploads directly there; the database stores only a row per image with its key, status and version. When the upload lands, an event goes onto a queue, and a pool of workers validates the file by its real bytes, strips EXIF but keeps orientation, runs moderation, resizes to a fixed set of widths and encodes WebP and AVIF. They write variants under a versioned path and then mark the row ready. Shoppers fetch images through a CDN with versioned, immutable URLs, so we cache for a year and never purge; replacing a photo just creates a new version. The page uses srcset so each phone downloads only the size it needs. Lifecycle rules clean up abandoned uploads, and every step is idempotent, so queue retries are safe."* **Likely follow-ups:** - *Eager resizing or on-the-fly?* Eager (all sizes made upfront) is predictable and cheap to serve. On-the-fly resizing behind the CDN suits new layouts, but the first request is slow and you must whitelist sizes to stop abuse. Many systems mix both. - *How do you handle a sale-day spike in uploads?* The queue absorbs the burst; workers autoscale on queue depth; seller-facing status shows "processing". Prioritise jobs for live listings over bulk catalogue imports with separate queues. ## Key takeaways - **Bytes in object storage, facts in the database.** Never store large images as database blobs at scale. - **Pre-signed URLs** let phones upload straight to storage; your API only authorises. - Heavy work runs **asynchronously** on a **queue with workers**: validate, strip EXIF, moderate, resize, encode WebP/AVIF. - Serve through a **CDN** with **versioned, immutable URLs**; change the URL instead of purging. - **Responsive images** (`srcset`, `sizes`, ``) so each device downloads only what it needs. - **Lifecycle rules** delete abandoned uploads and old versions, and move originals to cheaper storage. - Make every step **idempotent**: deterministic keys, conditional updates, retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue. ## Check yourself 1. Why give the phone a pre-signed URL instead of uploading through your API server? Answer: It sends large, slow uploads straight to object storage, which is built for them, so API servers don't hold the bytes in memory or tie up connections. The API still controls access by signing only one key, with a short expiry and type and size limits. 2. A seller replaces a product photo, but shoppers still see the old one for hours. What likely went wrong and how do you fix it? Answer: The new image was written to the same URL that the CDN and phones had cached with a long max-age. Write each change under a new versioned path and point the product at it, so caches fetch the new URL immediately and no purge is needed. 3. A queue delivers the same "process image" job twice. Why doesn't that create duplicate files or corrupt data? Answer: The worker writes variants to deterministic keys that include the image ID and version, so the second run overwrites identical files, and the final status update is conditional, so it changes nothing the second time. 4. Why strip EXIF metadata, and what must you do before stripping it? Answer: EXIF can contain private data like GPS location of the seller's home, plus it adds bytes. Before removing it, read the orientation tag and rotate the pixels, otherwise many photos will show up sideways.
title: Image upload pipelines

question: You type "samsng chargr" and the app still shows Samsung chargers. How does search handle typos?
answer:
## The short answer

Search handles typos by asking a simple question: **how many small edits would turn what you typed into a real word?** "samsng" is one edit away from "samsung" (add a "u"), and "chargr" is one edit away from "charger" (add an "e"). That count is called the **edit distance** (or **Levenshtein distance**). If a real word is only 1 or 2 edits away, the engine treats it as a likely match.

A real search system combines several tricks:

- **Fuzzy matching** with edit distance, done cleverly (n-gram indexes, BK-trees, or Lucene's automata) so it doesn't compare your query against millions of words one by one.
- **Spelling correction from query logs**: if lakhs of people typed "samsng" and then immediately searched "samsung", the system learns that correction ("Did you mean...").
- **Phonetic matching and transliteration**: "kurthi", "kurti" and "कुर्ती" should all find the same product.
- **Synonyms**: "chappal" should also find "slippers" and "flip-flops".
- **Ranking**: exact matches always beat fuzzy guesses.

And it has limits: very short words and model numbers ("iPhone 13" vs "iPhone 15") are dangerous to fuzz.

## The intuition

A shopkeeper hears "Samsng chargr" and hands over a Samsung charger, because (a) it sounds and looks nearly the same as a word he knows, and (b) he has heard this mistake a hundred times.

Search engines copy both habits. The "looks nearly the same" part is **edit distance**. The "heard it a hundred times" part is **learning from query logs**.

Terms used below:

- **Edit**: one small change to a word: insert a letter, delete a letter, or replace a letter.
- **Edit distance / Levenshtein distance**: the smallest number of edits needed to turn one word into another.
- **Dictionary / vocabulary**: the set of all words that appear in the product catalog (titles, brands, categories).
- **Fuzzy query**: a search that also accepts near-miss words.
- **N-gram**: a short chunk of N letters from a word. "charger" has trigrams (N = 3) "cha", "har", "arg", "rge", "ger".
- **Phonetic matching**: matching words that **sound** alike, even if spelled differently.
- **Transliteration**: writing a word from one script in another, such as Hindi "चप्पल" written in English letters as "chappal".

## How it actually works

### 1. Edit distance, step by step

We fill a small table using **dynamic programming** (solving a big problem by building up answers to smaller ones). Cell `D[i][j]` holds the edit distance between the first `i` letters of the typed word and the first `j` letters of the real word.

The rule for each cell:

- If the letters match, cost is 0, otherwise 1.
- `D[i][j] = min( D[i-1][j] + 1` (delete), `D[i][j-1] + 1` (insert), `D[i-1][j-1] + cost` (match or replace) `)`.

Worked table: a shopper types **"sari"**; the catalog says **"saree"**.

| | "" | s | a | r | e | e |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **""** | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| **s** | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| **a** | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| **r** | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| **i** | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | **1** | **2** |

How to read it:

- The first row and column mean "build this prefix from nothing": 0, 1, 2, 3...
- "sar" vs "sar" is 0 (all letters match, we walk down the diagonal).
- Row "i", column "e": "i" and "e" differ, so we replace: diagonal 0 + 1 = **1**. So "sari" vs "sare" is 1.
- Last cell: insert the final "e": left cell 1 + 1 = **2**.

The bottom-right cell is the answer: **"sari" is 2 edits from "saree"**. The table has (4+1) x (5+1) = 30 cells, so the cost is about length x length, written **O(m x n)**.

```java
static int editDistance(String a, String b) {
    int[] prev = new int[b.length() + 1], cur = new int[b.length() + 1];
    for (int j = 0; j <= b.length(); j++) prev[j] = j;
    for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
        cur[0] = i;
        for (int j = 1; j <= b.length(); j++) {
            int cost = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? 0 : 1;
            cur[j] = Math.min(Math.min(prev[j] + 1, cur[j - 1] + 1), prev[j - 1] + cost);
        }
        int[] t = prev; prev = cur; cur = t;   // keep only two rows: O(n) memory
    }
    return prev[b.length()];
}
```

A variant, **Damerau-Levenshtein**, counts swapping two neighbouring letters ("chagrer" to "charger") as **one** edit. Lucene does this by default.

### 2. Why "compare against every word" is too slow

A large catalog may have **several million distinct words** (brands, model numbers, colours, Hinglish words, seller misspellings). Each comparison is 50-100 cell updates, so one query means hundreds of millions of operations, against a budget of about **10-20 ms** at **tens of thousands of queries per second** during a sale. We need to look at only a tiny set of **candidate** words.

### 3. Shortcut A: n-gram index

Break every dictionary word into trigrams and keep a mini inverted index: trigram to words containing it.

- "chargr" has trigrams: cha, har, arg, rgr.
- "charger" has: cha, har, arg, rge, ger.
- They share 3 trigrams, so "charger" becomes a candidate quickly. "laptop" shares none and is never even looked at.

Run exact edit distance only on the top few hundred candidates. Simple, though short words have few trigrams.

### 4. Shortcut B: BK-tree

A **BK-tree** (Burkhard-Keller tree) stores words with each child edge labelled by its distance from the parent. Because edit distance obeys the **triangle inequality**, a search for words within 1 edit only follows edges labelled d - 1 to d + 1 (d = query's distance to the current node), skipping most branches. Good for small dictionaries; rare in large engines.

### 5. Shortcut C: Lucene's automaton-based fuzzy query

**Lucene** is the search library inside Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr. For a fuzzy query it builds a **Levenshtein automaton**: a small state machine that accepts exactly the strings within N edits of "samsng". Lucene stores its dictionary of terms in a sorted, compressed structure (an **FST**, finite state transducer). It walks the automaton and the term dictionary together, skipping whole ranges of terms that can't possibly match. The result: it visits only a few thousand terms instead of millions.

Practical knobs in Elasticsearch:

```json
{ "match": { "title": {
    "query": "samsng chargr",
    "fuzziness": "AUTO",
    "prefix_length": 1,
    "max_expansions": 50 } } }
```

- `fuzziness: AUTO` means 0 edits for words of 1-2 letters, 1 edit for 3-5 letters, 2 edits for 6+ letters. Lucene caps fuzziness at 2.
- `prefix_length: 1` assumes the first letter is right (people rarely get the first letter wrong), which cuts work a lot.
- `max_expansions` limits how many similar terms are tried.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Q[User types samsng chargr] --> N[Normalise and transliterate]
  N --> L[Query log correction]
  L --> S[Synonym expansion]
  S --> E[Exact match search]
  S --> F[Fuzzy match search]
  E --> R[Merge and rank]
  F --> R
  R --> U[Results and did you mean]
```

### 6. Spelling correction from query logs

Edit distance can't choose between equally close words ("shoo" is one edit from "shoe" and "shoot"). Logs settle it. The classic idea is the **noisy channel model**: pick the correction `c` that maximises **P(c) x P(typed | c)**, where P(c) is how popular the intended word is, and P(typed | c) is how likely that typo is.

Where the data comes from:

- **Reformulations**: a user types "samsng chargr", gets few clicks, and within 10 seconds types "samsung charger" and clicks. Millions of such pairs teach a mapping.
- **Clicks and popularity**: if people searching "addidas" click Adidas shoes, that's strong evidence.

Two levels of confidence:

- **High confidence**: silently rewrite the query and show "Showing results for samsung charger. Search instead for samsng chargr".
- **Medium confidence**: show the original results plus "Did you mean: samsung charger?"

Corrections are precomputed offline into a typo-to-correction table, so serving is a fast lookup.

### 7. Phonetic matching and transliteration for Indian users

Indian shoppers often type Hindi, Tamil or other words in English letters, and there is **no single correct spelling**. "kurti", "kurthi", "kurtee"; "chappal", "chapal", "chappel"; "jhumka", "jumka". Edit distance helps a bit, but sound-based tricks help more:

- **Phonetic codes**: algorithms such as **Soundex** or **Metaphone** reduce a word to a sound key (drop vowels, merge letters that sound alike). Words with the same key match. These were built for English names, so Indian systems usually add **custom rules**: "th" and "t" are the same, "ee" and "i" are the same, double letters collapse ("pp" to "p"), "w" and "v" merge.
- **Transliteration**: convert Devanagari or Tamil script queries ("चप्पल") into a common Latin form, or index products under both forms.
- **Hinglish dictionaries**: map common Hinglish words to catalog terms: "chappal" to slippers, "kurti" to women's tunic, "jhola" to tote bag.

Example normalisation rules (pseudocode):

```
normalise(w):
  w = lowercase(w)
  w = replace(w, "th", "t"); w = replace(w, "ee", "i"); w = replace(w, "oo", "u")
  w = collapse_double_letters(w)     # chappal -> chapal
  return w
# kurthi -> kurti, chappel -> chapel (then fuzzy 1 edit finds chapal)
```

### 8. Synonyms

People also use different **words** for the same thing: "mobile" vs "phone", "fridge" vs "refrigerator", "chappal" vs "flip-flops". A **synonym list** (curated plus mined from logs) expands the query. Make synonyms **directional** where needed: "iphone" can expand to "apple phone", but "apple" should not become "iphone" (it might mean the fruit).

### 9. Ranking: exact beats fuzzy

Fuzzy matching is forgiving but noisy, so ranking prefers stronger evidence:

| Match type | Example for query "kurti" | Score boost |
|---|---|---|
| Exact term | kurti | highest |
| Synonym | tunic | high |
| Phonetic or transliterated | kurthi | medium |
| Fuzzy, 1 edit | kurta | lower |
| Fuzzy, 2 edits | kurtis? curtain? | lowest |

In Elasticsearch this is often done by running an exact clause and a fuzzy clause together and giving the exact one a higher boost. Business signals (sales, ratings, stock) then reorder within each tier.

### 10. The limits

- **Short words**: "tv" is one edit from "tb", "ac" from "ab". This is why `AUTO` allows **zero** edits for 1-2 letter words.
- **Model numbers and codes**: "iphone 13" is one edit from "iphone 15", and "5g" from "4g". Fuzzing these shows the **wrong product**. Many systems turn fuzziness off for tokens with digits.

## A worked example

**A shopper on a Flipkart-like app types "samsng chargr" during a big sale.**

1. **Normalise** (lowercase, trim): still "samsng chargr".
2. **Query-log lookup**: the precomputed correction table has "samsng" to "samsung" (seen 40,000 times last month, 92% of those users then clicked Samsung products) and "chargr" to "charger". Confidence is high, so the query becomes "samsung charger" and the UI shows "Showing results for samsung charger".
3. **Synonym expansion**: "charger" also matches "adapter" and "power adapter" in the mobile accessories category.
4. **Search**: Elasticsearch runs an exact clause on "samsung charger" (boost 3) and a fuzzy clause on the original words with fuzziness AUTO and prefix_length 1 (boost 1), as a safety net in case the correction was wrong.
5. **Ranking**: Samsung 25W chargers that match exactly rank first, sorted by rating, sales and stock. Generic "charger for Samsung" listings come next.
6. **Second shopper**, same night, types "kurthi cotton". There's no log entry for this exact pair, but **phonetic normalisation** maps "kurthi" to "kurti", which matches. Results show cotton kurtis.
7. **Third shopper** types "iphone 13". Fuzzy is **off for tokens with digits**, so iPhone 15 never sneaks in.

Steps 1-5 take roughly 15-30 ms: corrections are a hash lookup, and the automaton touches only a few thousand terms.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Fuzzy search compares the query to every word."** No. That's far too slow at scale. Engines use n-gram indexes, BK-trees, or Levenshtein automata to visit only a small candidate set.
- **"Bigger edit distance is always more helpful."** Beyond 2 edits, almost everything matches everything ("shoe" is 2 edits from "show", "shop", "hose"). Lucene caps it at 2 for good reason.
- **"Spelling correction is just edit distance."** Edit distance finds candidates; **query logs and popularity** decide which candidate the user meant.
- **"English spellcheck works for Indian users."** It misses Hinglish, regional words and other scripts; add transliteration and local phonetic rules.
- **"Fuzzy matching is safe everywhere."** Model numbers, sizes and short words break badly. Turn it off or tighten it there.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Search handles typos in layers. The base idea is edit distance, or Levenshtein distance: the minimum number of inserts, deletes or replacements to turn one word into another, computed with a small dynamic programming table in length times length time. Comparing against millions of catalog words is too slow, so engines prune candidates first: an n-gram index, a BK-tree, or, in Lucene and Elasticsearch, a Levenshtein automaton that walks the term dictionary and skips anything that can't be within one or two edits. On top of that, the best signal is query logs: if many users type samsng and then search samsung and click, we precompute that correction and show results for it or a did-you-mean. For Indian users we add transliteration and phonetic normalisation so kurthi, kurti and the Hindi script version all match, plus synonyms like chappal to slippers. Ranking always puts exact matches above fuzzy ones. And we limit fuzziness: none for one or two letter words, and none for model numbers, so iPhone 13 never turns into iPhone 15."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *How do you pick between two equally close corrections?* Use popularity and context from logs, the noisy channel idea: the more common word, and the one users actually clicked after retyping, wins. Neighbouring words help too ("shoo polish" means shoe).
- *How do you measure if correction works?* Zero-result rate, quick-reformulation rate, and click-through on corrected queries, validated with an A/B test.
- *Fuzzy search is adding latency during a sale. What do you do?* Run exact first and fuzzy only when results are few, raise prefix_length, lower max_expansions, and rely more on the precomputed correction table.

## Key takeaways

- **Edit distance** counts the minimum inserts, deletes and replacements; a small DP table computes it in O(m x n).
- Comparing a query against **every** dictionary word is far too slow; use **n-grams, BK-trees or Lucene's Levenshtein automata** to find candidates.
- Keep fuzziness small: **0 for very short words, 1-2 edits otherwise**, and require the first letter to match.
- **Query logs** are the strongest correction signal: reformulations plus clicks give "did you mean".
- For Indian users, add **transliteration, phonetic rules and Hinglish dictionaries**.
- **Synonyms** handle different words for the same thing; make them directional.
- **Rank exact above synonym above phonetic above fuzzy.**
- **Don't fuzz model numbers, sizes or short tokens.**

## Check yourself

1. What is the edit distance between "chargr" and "charger", and which single edit gets you there?
   Answer: 1. Insert the letter "e" between "g" and "r".
2. Why does Elasticsearch's fuzziness AUTO allow zero edits for a two-letter word like "tv"?
   Answer: With so few letters, one edit turns it into many unrelated words ("tb", "to", "ac" from "ab"), so fuzzy matches would mostly be wrong.
3. Two words are both 1 edit from what the user typed. How does a production system choose?
   Answer: It uses query logs and popularity: which word users most often meant (seen through reformulations and clicks), plus the context of nearby words.
4. A shopper types "kurthi". Which technique is most likely to find kurtis, and why not plain fuzzy alone?
   Answer: Phonetic normalisation ("th" to "t") or a Hinglish dictionary. Plain fuzzy also finds it at 1 edit, but phonetic rules handle many spellings consistently and with higher confidence.
title: Fuzzy search and typos

question: A delivery agent marks orders as delivered while in a basement with no network. How does the app save that and sync it later without losing or mixing up data?
answer:
## The short answer

The app never waits for the network to say "saved". When the agent taps **Mark delivered**, the app writes the change into a **local database on the phone** first, and at the same moment adds a small record to an **outbox**: a queue of changes still waiting to go to the server. The screen updates right away.

When the network comes back, a **sync worker** sends outbox items to the server, oldest first, and **retries** on failure. Each item carries a unique **idempotency key**, so if the same request reaches the server twice, it is applied only once. Nothing is lost (it is on disk) and nothing is applied twice (the key de-duplicates).

"Mixed up" data is handled in two ways:
- **Ordering**: each change carries a per-device sequence number, so the server applies them in the order they happened. Phone clocks can be wrong, so the clock time is only a hint.
- **Conflicts**: if the same order was changed on the server meanwhile (say, the customer cancelled), the server spots it with a **version number** and resolves it with a rule per field: **last-write-wins**, **server-wins**, **merge**, or **ask a human**.

The UI shows what is going on: "Saved on phone, 3 changes waiting to sync", then a tick when the server confirms.

## The intuition

Think of a courier in an old building with no signal. He cannot call the office after each drop. So he writes each delivery in a **paper notebook**, with the time and a line number: "Line 7, order 4471, delivered, 2:14 pm". When he walks out to the street and gets signal, he reads out every line not yet ticked to the office and ticks each one after the office says "noted".

- If the call drops halfway, he simply reads the unticked lines again. The office keeps a list of line numbers it has already noted, so a repeated line is ignored. That is the **idempotency key**.
- If the office says "wait, the customer cancelled 4471 at 2:10 pm", someone must decide which fact wins. That is **conflict resolution**.
- If his watch is fast, the line numbers still show the true order. That is why we prefer **sequence numbers** over clock time.

Terms:
- **Offline-first**: the app is designed to work fully without network; the network is used when available, not required.
- **Local database**: storage on the phone (SQLite, Room on Android, Core Data on iOS, IndexedDB in a web app). It survives app restarts and phone reboots.
- **Outbox**: a table of pending changes, written together with the data change.
- **Idempotent**: doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once.
- **Conflict**: two parties changed the same thing without seeing each other's change.
- **Version number**: a counter on a record that goes up by one on every change; used to detect conflicts.

## How it actually works

### 1. Write locally first, in one transaction

The key rule: **the data change and its outbox entry are saved together, in one local transaction**. Either both are on disk or neither is. This is the same idea as the server-side transactional outbox, just on the phone.

```java
db.runInTransaction(() -> {
    orderDao.updateStatus("OD4471", "DELIVERED", podPhotoPath);
    outboxDao.insert(new OutboxItem(
        UUID.randomUUID().toString(),   // idempotency key
        nextSeq(),                      // per-device sequence: 41, 42, 43...
        "OD4471", "MARK_DELIVERED",
        baseVersion,                    // version the agent saw, e.g. 7
        System.currentTimeMillis(),     // device time: a hint only
        payloadJson));
});
```

If the app crashes one millisecond later, both rows are still there. If we wrote the order first and queued the request in memory, a crash would lose the request.

### 2. The outbox and the sync worker

The outbox is a plain table: `id`, `seq`, `entity_id`, `op`, `base_version`, `created_at`, `payload`, `status`, `attempts`. A background worker (WorkManager on Android, BGTaskScheduler on iOS) runs when the OS reports network is available:

1. Read pending items in `seq` order, in batches (say 20).
2. Send them to the server.
3. On success, mark them done (or delete them) and save the server's new version for each order.
4. On failure, leave them pending and retry later.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Agent taps Delivered] --> B[Local DB plus outbox]
    B --> C[UI shows pending]
    C --> D{Network up?}
    D -->|No| E[Wait and retry later]
    E --> D
    D -->|Yes| F[Send batch to server]
    F --> G{Server reply}
    G -->|OK| H[Mark synced]
    G -->|Conflict| I[Resolve by rule]
    I --> H
```

### 3. Retries with backoff

Retry with **exponential backoff plus jitter**: wait 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, up to a cap of a few minutes, plus a small random amount so 50,000 agents leaving a metro station don't all hit the server in the same second. Retry only **temporary** errors (timeouts, 503). A **permanent** error (400, a validation failure) goes to a "needs attention" state, not into an endless loop.

### 4. Idempotency keys

Here is the classic trap: the phone sends "OD4471 delivered", the server saves it, and the reply is lost as the agent steps back into the lift. The phone thinks it failed and sends again. Without protection, the server might record two deliveries, pay the agent twice, or send the customer two "delivered" SMSes.

The fix: the server stores each processed **idempotency key** (in a table with a unique constraint, kept for some days). If a key arrives again, it returns the **saved earlier result** and does nothing new. The key is created **once, when the change is made**, not on each retry; otherwise every retry looks new.

### 5. Ordering and timestamps

Phone clocks are unreliable. Users set them by hand, batteries die and reset them, time zones change mid-journey. A phone can easily be 10 minutes off, sometimes hours. So:

- **Order within one device** with the **sequence number** (41, 42, 43). It never goes backwards, whatever the clock says.
- **Record two times**: the device time (when the agent says it happened, useful for reports and disputes) and the **server receive time** (trustworthy). The server can also estimate the clock skew at sync time.
- **Never let a wrong clock decide a conflict alone.** If "latest timestamp wins" uses phone time, a phone set to next year wins every argument.

### 6. Conflicts and version numbers

Each order on the server has a `version`. The phone remembers the version it last saw (say 7) and sends it as `base_version`. The server checks:

- Current version still 7: no one else changed it. Apply, set version 8, reply OK.
- Current version is 9: someone changed it meanwhile. That's a **conflict**.

This is **optimistic concurrency**: no locks, just "apply only if nothing changed since I looked". Then a rule decides the outcome:

| Strategy | How it works | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Last-write-wins (LWW)** | Latest change replaces the earlier one | Low-stakes fields: agent's notes, display preferences |
| **Server-wins** | Server value is kept, phone change is rejected | Money and authority fields: price, refund status, cancellation |
| **Merge** | Combine changes to different fields, or add both to a list | Independent fields: agent adds photo, customer edits landmark |
| **Ask the user** | Show both versions, a human decides | Rare, high-value cases; use sparingly in a delivery app |

Real systems mix these **per field**, not one rule for the whole record. Also, a **domain rule** often beats a generic one: "delivered" is a physical fact backed by a photo and GPS, so a later "cancel" from the customer cannot undo it; it should become a return request instead.

### 7. CRDTs, in one paragraph

**CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)** are data structures designed so that any two copies can always be merged automatically, in any order, and end up the same. Examples: a counter where each device keeps its own count and the total is the sum, or the text structures behind collaborative editors (Automerge, Yjs). They are excellent for **collaborative editing and offline notes**. For delivery status they are usually overkill, because the business rules ("cancel after delivery becomes a return") are not things a generic merge can decide. Know what they are; reach for them when many people edit the same data offline.

### 8. Showing sync status in the UI

Honesty in the UI prevents panic and double work:
- Per item: a small clock icon for "saved on phone", a tick for "synced", a red mark for "needs attention".
- A banner: "Offline. 3 deliveries saved, will sync automatically."
- A "Sync now" button and a clear message when something is rejected.
- **Block logout or app data clear while items are pending**, or warn loudly, because that is one of the few ways to really lose data.

## A worked example

**A Flipkart-like delivery app, festive sale week, a large apartment complex in Chennai.**

1. Ravi, the delivery agent, enters a basement parking area with no signal. He has 6 parcels for the tower. Phone clock is 9 minutes fast.
2. For order OD4471 he scans the parcel, takes a proof-of-delivery photo, and taps Delivered. The app writes, in one SQLite transaction: order status `DELIVERED`, photo path, and an outbox row with key `k-91c2`, `seq = 41`, `base_version = 7`. The screen shows a clock icon. Total time: about 30 ms.
3. He delivers 4 more (seq 42 to 45). For OD4480 the customer refuses, so he marks it `RETURNED` (seq 46). The banner reads "Offline. 6 changes saved."
4. Meanwhile, at 2:10 pm server time, customer support changed OD4480's delivery slot (version 4 to 5), and the customer of OD4471 tried to cancel (version 7 to 8) but the cancel was put on hold because the parcel was already out for delivery.
5. Ravi comes up to the ground floor. Android reports the network; the sync worker sends seq 41 to 46 as one batch. The reply is lost when he steps into the lift. Backoff: retry after 2 s, then 4 s. The second retry succeeds.
6. The server sees keys `k-91c2` and others. Seq 42 to 45 were already applied by the first (lost) attempt, so it returns the saved results: **no double delivery, no double payout**.
7. OD4471: base version 7, server version 8, a conflict. The **domain rule** applies: delivery with a photo is a fact, so status becomes `DELIVERED` (version 9), and the pending cancel becomes a return request. Ravi's phone is told the new version.
8. OD4480: base version 4, server version 5. The fields are different (status vs slot), so the server **merges**: status `RETURNED`, slot unchanged.
9. All device times are about 9 minutes ahead of server receive times. The server notes the skew and stores corrected times for reports, but nothing relied on them for ordering.
10. Ravi's screen shows 6 ticks: nothing lost, nothing duplicated, two conflicts settled by clear rules.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Phone
    participant S as Server
    P->>S: batch seq 41 to 46
    S-->>P: reply lost
    P->>S: retry same keys
    S->>S: 42 to 45 already done
    S->>S: 4471 conflict, rule applied
    S-->>P: OK with new versions
```

## Common misconceptions

- **"Just retry the HTTP call until it works."** If the app is killed or the phone reboots, an in-memory retry is gone. Pending changes must be **on disk**, in the outbox.
- **"Retries are safe by default."** Not for creating or changing things. Without an **idempotency key**, a lost reply plus a retry can apply the change twice.
- **"Use the phone's timestamp to decide who wins."** Phone clocks are often wrong. Use **sequence numbers** for order and **server versions** for conflicts; keep device time as a hint.
- **"Last-write-wins is always fine."** It silently throws away the other change. For money, status and safety fields, use **server-wins or domain rules**.
- **"CRDTs solve all sync problems."** They guarantee copies converge, not that the result makes business sense. Most business workflows still need explicit rules.

## How to say it in an interview

*"I'd design it offline-first. When the agent taps Delivered, the app writes the status change and an outbox entry in one local SQLite transaction, so the change survives crashes and reboots, and the UI updates immediately with a pending marker. A background sync worker sends outbox items in order when the network returns, with exponential backoff and jitter. Each change gets an idempotency key when it is created, and the server stores processed keys, so a retry after a lost reply is not applied twice. For ordering, I use a per-device sequence number, because phone clocks can be badly wrong; device time is kept as a hint and the server records its own receive time. For conflicts, each record has a version number; the phone sends the version it based its change on, and if the server has moved on, a per-field rule decides: last-write-wins for low-risk fields, server-wins for money and cancellation, merge for independent fields, and a domain rule that delivered with proof beats a later cancel. CRDTs are an option for collaborative data, but overkill here. Finally, the UI shows saved, synced and needs-attention states, and warns before logout with pending items."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *What if the outbox grows very large, say after a day offline?* Send in batches, compress photos and upload them separately with their own keys, and collapse redundant changes to the same order before sending (only the latest status matters if nothing depends on the steps).
- *How long does the server keep idempotency keys?* Longer than the longest realistic offline period plus retries, for example 7 to 30 days; after that, version checks still protect against most stale replays.
- *How do you test this?* Airplane mode, killing the app mid-sync, dropping replies after commit, wrong clocks, and conflicting edits from two clients.

## Key takeaways

- **Write to the local database first**; the network is never on the critical path of a tap.
- Save the change and its **outbox entry in one local transaction**.
- A **sync worker** sends pending items in order, with **backoff and jitter**, and only retries temporary errors.
- **Idempotency keys**, created once per change, stop duplicates after lost replies.
- **Don't trust device clocks** for ordering; use **per-device sequence numbers** and server time.
- **Version numbers** detect conflicts; resolve them **per field**: LWW, server-wins, merge, or ask a human, plus domain rules.
- **CRDTs** merge automatically and suit collaborative editing, but don't replace business rules.
- Show **sync status** honestly: saved locally, synced, needs attention.

## Check yourself

1. The app updates the order row on the phone, then crashes before adding the outbox entry. What went wrong in the design, and how do you fix it?
   Answer: The two writes were separate, so the change exists locally but will never be sent. Write the data change and the outbox entry in one local transaction so both are saved or neither is.
2. The server applies "OD4471 delivered", but the reply is lost and the phone retries. Why must the idempotency key be generated when the change is created, not when the request is sent?
   Answer: If a new key were generated per attempt, the retry would look like a brand-new change and be applied again. A key fixed at creation time lets the server recognise the retry and return the earlier result.
3. A phone's clock is set two days ahead. Under "latest timestamp wins", what goes wrong, and what should be used instead?
   Answer: Every change from that phone would win every conflict, even when it is actually older. Use per-device sequence numbers for ordering and server version numbers to detect conflicts, keeping device time only as a hint.
4. The agent marks an order delivered offline; meanwhile the customer cancels it on the server. Which conflict strategy fits, and why not plain last-write-wins?
   Answer: A domain rule (or server-side rule) that a delivery with proof is a physical fact, so it stays delivered and the cancel becomes a return. Last-write-wins would decide based on timing alone and could silently cancel a delivered parcel or drop the customer's request.
title: Offline save and sync

question: How can five people type in the same Google Doc at the same time without overwriting each other's words?
answer:
## The short answer

Five people can type in the same Google Docs-like document at once because the editor **never sends the whole document around**. Each keystroke becomes a tiny **operation** such as "insert x at position 5" or "delete the character at position 12". Your screen applies your own operation **instantly**, and the operation is also sent to the others.

The hard part: while your operation travels, someone else may have typed earlier in the document, so "position 5" now points at the wrong place. Two main techniques fix this:

- **Operational Transformation (OT):** before applying someone else's operation, **adjust (transform) its position** to account for edits that happened at the same time. A **central server** puts all operations in one agreed order. Google Docs is widely reported to use this approach.
- **CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types):** give every character a **unique, permanent ID** instead of a number position, and say "insert after character ID such-and-such". Then edits can be **merged in any order** and everyone still ends up with the same text.

## The intuition

Imagine five friends writing one shopping list on a shared whiteboard, but each has their own copy in a different room and can only pass **sticky notes** through a messenger.

Sending a photo of the whole list would let the last photo **wipe out** others' changes. So they send small notes: "add milk on line 3".

Now a problem. Priya adds "eggs" on line 1. At the same moment Arjun sends "add milk on line 3". When Arjun's note reaches Priya, her list has shifted down by one line, so "line 3" means a different spot. Priya needs to think: "Someone (me) added a line above line 3 at the same time, so Arjun really meant line 4." That small correction is **transformation**.

The other approach: give every item on the list a **name tag** that never changes. Arjun's note says "add milk right after the tag called bread-7". No matter how many lines move, everyone finds bread-7 and puts milk after it. That is the **CRDT** idea.

Terms:
- **Operation (op):** one small change, like insert or delete, with a position.
- **Concurrent edits:** two edits made at the same time, where neither person had seen the other's edit yet.
- **Converge:** everyone ends with exactly the same document.
- **Replica:** one copy of the document, on one person's device.
- **Latency:** the delay for a message to travel, often 50 to 300 ms on mobile networks.

## How it actually works

### 1. Why "send the whole document" fails

The naive design: every few seconds, upload the full text, and the server keeps the latest copy.

- **Lost updates:** Priya and Arjun both download version 10. Priya uploads her version, then Arjun uploads his. Arjun's upload **overwrites** Priya's words because his copy never had them. This is the classic **last write wins** problem.
- **Locking does not help:** lock the document while one person types, and four people wait.
- **It is wasteful:** a 200 KB document sent on every keystroke, for a few bytes of change.

So we send **operations**, which are tiny (a few dozen bytes each), and design rules so they can be combined safely.

### 2. Operations, applied locally first

Each change is a small message:

```
{ "type": "insert", "pos": 5, "text": "x", "user": "priya", "baseRev": 41 }
{ "type": "delete", "pos": 12, "len": 1,  "user": "arjun", "baseRev": 41 }
```

`baseRev` means "I made this edit while looking at revision 41 of the document".

The editor applies your op **on your screen immediately** (called **optimistic local apply**), so typing never feels slow. Then it sends the op to the server in the background. 

### 3. The conflict, with a tiny example

The document is `PAN`. Positions start at 0: P=0, A=1, N=2.

- Asha types `S` at the start: **insert S at 0**. Her screen shows `SPAN`.
- At the same moment, Ravi types `E` at the end: **insert E at 3**. His screen shows `PANE`.

Now each receives the other's op.

- Ravi applies Asha's "insert S at 0" to `PANE` and gets `SPANE`. Correct.
- Asha applies Ravi's "insert E at 3" to `SPAN` and gets `SPAEN`. **Wrong**, because her S shifted everything right by one.

The two screens now **disagree**, and will keep drifting apart. This is the core problem.

### 4. Operational Transformation (OT)

OT fixes this with a **transform function**: given two concurrent ops, adjust one so it still means the same thing after the other has been applied.

For two inserts, the rule is simple: if the other insert landed **before** my position, shift my position right by its length.

```java
record Insert(int pos, String text, String userId) {}

// Rewrite op 'a' so it can be applied after concurrent op 'b' has already been applied.
static Insert transform(Insert a, Insert b) {
    boolean bComesFirst = b.pos() < a.pos()
        || (b.pos() == a.pos() && b.userId().compareTo(a.userId()) < 0); // tie-break
    return bComesFirst
        ? new Insert(a.pos() + b.text().length(), a.text(), a.userId())
        : a;
}
```

In our example, Ravi's "insert E at 3" is transformed against Asha's "insert S at 0". Since 0 is before 3, it becomes **insert E at 4**, and Asha's screen shows `SPANE`. Both screens match.

The **tie-break** matters: if both type at the same position, a fixed rule (here, compare user IDs) decides who goes first, so every replica makes the same choice. Real editors need similar rules for deletes (a delete before you shifts you **left**) and formatting.

**Why a central server?** Transforming ops correctly when many people edit in any order, peer to peer, is famously hard; several published OT algorithms were later shown to have bugs in tricky cases. The practical fix, used by Google Docs-like systems, is a **central server that decides one official order**:

1. The client sends its op with `baseRev = 41`.
2. The server has already accepted revisions 42 and 43 from others. It **transforms** the incoming op against 42 and 43, stores it as **revision 44**, and broadcasts it.
3. Each client transforms the incoming revision 44 against any of its own ops that are still waiting for an acknowledgement, then applies it.
4. A client usually keeps **only one batch of ops in flight**, buffering the rest, to keep its logic simple.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Asha types S] --> B[Apply on Asha screen]
    C[Ravi types E] --> D[Apply on Ravi screen]
    B --> E[Send op to server]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Server picks one order]
    F --> G[Transform later op]
    G --> H[Save as next revision]
    H --> I[Broadcast to all editors]
    I --> J[Everyone shows SPANE]
```

### 5. CRDTs: the alternative

A **CRDT** avoids transforming positions at all. Instead of "insert at position 3", every character gets a **unique ID**, for example `(counter, userId)` like `7@ravi`, and every insert says "**put this after the character with ID X**".

- Asha inserts S after the special START marker.
- Ravi inserts E after the character `N`, whose ID is, say, `3@asha`.

Positions never appear in the op, so no shifting is needed. If two people insert after the **same** character, a fixed tie-break on the IDs decides the order, the same on every device.

**Deletes** usually leave a **tombstone**: the character is marked deleted but its ID stays, because another person's insert might still say "after this character". Tombstones are cleaned up later (garbage collection) when it is safe.

The big property: CRDT ops can be **applied in any order, even twice**, and every replica ends identical, so no central server is strictly needed. Open-source libraries such as **Yjs** and **Automerge** implement this.

### 6. OT vs CRDT trade-offs

| | OT | CRDT |
|---|---|---|
| Position model | Numbers, shifted by transforms | Unique IDs per character |
| Needs central server | Practically yes | No, but often uses one anyway |
| Offline and peer to peer | Harder, long offline edits need many transforms | Natural fit |
| Memory | Plain text plus op log | Extra ID per character plus tombstones |
| Maturity | Decades of production use | Mature libraries now, newer at huge scale |
| Correctness risk | Transform functions are subtle | Merge is simpler to prove correct |

Neither is better in general: mostly-online products with a strong server fit OT; offline-heavy apps fit CRDTs.

### 7. Cursors and presence

**Presence** means showing who is in the document and where their cursor is (the coloured flags with names).

- Cursor positions are sent as small, **frequent but throwaway** messages, often throttled to a few per second.
- They are **not saved** in the document history. If one is lost, the next one corrects it.
- A cursor position is itself a position, so it is **transformed** (OT) or anchored to a character ID (CRDT), otherwise Ravi's cursor would jump when Asha types above it.
- Usually carried over a **WebSocket** (a long-lived two-way connection).

### 8. Offline edits

When the network drops, the editor keeps applying your ops locally and **queues** them. On reconnect:

- **OT:** the client sends its queued ops with the old `baseRev`; the server transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile. This works but gets expensive and edge-case heavy after hours of separate editing.
- **CRDT:** the client just exchanges missing ops; merge works in any order.

Either way, the merge is **automatic but not magic**: if two people rewrite the same sentence differently, both texts survive in some interleaved form. The system guarantees everyone sees the **same** result, not that the result reads well. Humans fix the meaning.

### 9. Version history

The server's ordered **op log** lets it rebuild any revision by replaying ops. To keep that fast, it saves periodic **snapshots** (the full text every few hundred revisions) and replays only from the nearest snapshot. History groups nearby ops by author and time instead of showing every keystroke.

## A worked example

**A Flipkart-like marketplace team edits the festive sale launch plan.** Five people (the programme manager, two category leads, a marketing writer and an engineering lead) open the same Google Docs-like document at 10 am, the day before the sale freeze.

1. **Opening:** each browser loads the latest snapshot plus recent ops (say revision 2,310), opens a WebSocket, and starts sending presence. Everyone sees five coloured cursors.
2. **Typing:** the electronics lead adds "Phones: 40% off" in section 3. The op `insert at 1,204` is applied on her screen instantly and sent to the server.
3. **Concurrent edit:** simultaneously the programme manager inserts 30 characters at position 150. His op reaches the server first: revision 2,311.
4. **Transform:** the electronics lead's op arrives with `baseRev 2,310`. The server sees revision 2,311 inserted 30 characters before position 1,204, so it transforms her op to **insert at 1,234**, stores it as revision 2,312, and broadcasts it. All five screens match.
5. **Same spot:** two people type at the end of one sentence. The tie-break puts one first on every screen; **no words are lost**.
6. **Offline:** the engineering lead is on a train with no network for 20 minutes. He keeps editing the rollback section; his ops queue locally. On reconnect, they are sent with the old base revision, transformed against roughly 400 newer revisions, and merged. 
7. **Mistake and recovery:** at 4 pm someone accidentally deletes the whole pricing table. The programme manager opens **version history**, finds the 3:55 pm version (rebuilt from a snapshot plus replayed ops), and restores it. The restore is itself a new set of ops.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The server just keeps the latest full copy."** That causes lost updates. Real-time editors exchange small operations and merge them.
- **"OT and CRDT guarantee the text makes sense."** They guarantee **convergence** (everyone sees the same thing) and keep each person's characters. If two people rewrite one sentence, the result can still be messy; people resolve meaning.
- **"CRDTs are always better than OT."** CRDTs make offline and peer-to-peer easier but cost extra memory per character and tombstones. OT with a central server is proven at very large scale. It depends on the product.
- **"Your typing waits for the server."** No. Ops are applied locally first; the server only decides the final order and the transform keeps everyone consistent.

## How to say it in an interview

*"Sending the whole document fails because the last upload overwrites everyone else. So a collaborative editor sends small operations, like insert x at position 5, and applies your own op on your screen immediately. The problem is that positions shift: if someone inserts text earlier in the document at the same time, your position 5 now points somewhere else. Operational Transformation fixes this by adjusting each op against concurrent ops, for example shifting an insert right if another insert landed before it, with a fixed tie-break for the same spot. A central server puts all ops in one order and broadcasts them; Google Docs is widely reported to work this way. The alternative is a CRDT, where every character has a unique ID and inserts say put this after character X, so ops merge in any order, which is great for offline and peer to peer, at the cost of extra metadata. On top of that you add presence over WebSockets, an offline queue, and an op log with snapshots for version history."*

**Likely follow-ups:**
- *What happens if two people type at exactly the same position?* A deterministic tie-break, such as comparing user or site IDs, puts one first. Every replica applies the same rule, so they converge.
- *Why does OT usually need a central server?* Transforming ops correctly in every possible order between many peers is very hard to get right. A server that fixes one global order reduces it to transforming against a known list.
- *When would you choose a CRDT?* When offline editing or peer-to-peer sync matters a lot, such as a field app or a local-first notes app, and you can afford extra memory per character.

## Key takeaways

- Sending the **whole document** leads to **lost updates**; send **small operations** instead.
- Apply your own op **locally first**, so typing never waits for the network.
- Concurrent edits make **positions shift**; without a fix, replicas **diverge**.
- **OT** transforms each op against concurrent ops, with a **central server** setting one order. Google Docs is widely reported to use OT.
- **CRDTs** use **unique character IDs** and "insert after X", so ops **merge in any order**; good for offline, costs memory and tombstones.
- A **deterministic tie-break** makes same-spot edits converge.
- **Presence** (cursors) is separate, throwaway data, but still needs position adjusting.
- An **op log plus snapshots** gives version history and safe restores.

## Check yourself

1. Two people download version 10 of a document, edit, and upload the full text. What goes wrong?
   Answer: The second upload overwrites the first, because the second person's copy never contained the first person's changes. This is a lost update, which is why editors send operations instead.
2. The text is `CAT`. Meena inserts `S` at position 3 while Kabir inserts `B` at position 0. Using OT, what op does Meena's insert become after Kabir's, and what is the final text?
   Answer: Kabir's insert is at 0, before 3, so Meena's op becomes insert S at 4. Both screens show `BCATS`.
3. Why does a CRDT not need to transform positions?
   Answer: Its ops refer to unique character IDs, such as insert after character 3 by Asha, not to numeric positions. IDs never shift, so ops can be applied in any order and still give the same result.
4. Why are cursor positions not stored in version history, and what must still happen to them when others type?
   Answer: Cursors are short-lived presence data; losing one is harmless because the next update corrects it, so saving them would only bloat history. They must still be transformed or anchored to character IDs so they do not jump when text is inserted before them.
title: Real-time collaborative editing

question: Why can't you run "total sales by city for the last year" on the same database that takes orders? OLTP vs OLAP, data warehouses and data lakes explained.
answer:
## The short answer

The two jobs want **opposite things** from a database.

- The database that takes orders is an **OLTP** system (Online Transaction Processing). It handles **many tiny, fast requests**: "insert this order", "reduce stock of this item by 1", "show order 4471". Each must finish in milliseconds.
- "Total sales by city for the last year" is an **OLAP** query (Online Analytical Processing). It is **one huge request**: read hundreds of millions of rows, add them up, group them. 
If you run the big report on the order database, it **competes for the same CPU, disk, memory and locks** as checkout. Checkout gets slow or times out, and customers leave. It is also **built the wrong way** for this: it stores data **row by row**, so it reads every column when you need three.

So companies **copy the data** out of the order database into a separate system built for analysis: a **data warehouse** (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift-style), a **data lake** (cheap raw files), or a mix of both called a **lakehouse**. The copy is made by **ETL** jobs or **CDC** streams, and the price you pay is **freshness**: the report is a few minutes or hours behind reality.

## The intuition
